﴿To God belongs the command, before and after, and on that day the believers will rejoice﴾

Then He Most High said, ﴿To God belongs the command, before and after﴾, meaning before the victory and after it, or before this period and after it. That is, if He willed to make them victorious, He would make them victorious before a few years, and if He willed to make them victorious after them, He would do so. He did not determine this period out of incapacity. Rather, it is an effective will. Both words (qabl and ba'd) are built on the dammah (ḍamm) when they are cut off from the genitive construction (idafah), because the other vowels, the fathah and the kasrah, would be confused with what enters upon them, which is the accusative (nasb) and the genitive (jarr). As for the accusative, it is in your saying, "I came before him or after him." As for the genitive, it is in your saying, "from before him and from after him." So they are built on the dammah, because their like does not enter upon them in the case-marking (i'rab) of the nominative (raf'). ﴿And on that day the believers will rejoice﴾. It has been said that they will rejoice at the victory of the Romans over the Persians, just as the polytheists rejoiced at the victory of the Persians over the Romans. The more correct view is that they will rejoice at their own victory over the polytheists. This is because the victory of the Romans happened on the same day as the victory of the Muslims over the polytheists at Badr. If what they mentioned were intended, it would not be correct, because on that very day the news of the Romans' defeat had not yet reached them, so their rejoicing would not be on that day. Rather, the rejoicing occurs after that.

* * *

* * *

* * *
Then God Most High said: ﴿They know an outward aspect of the worldly life﴾. That is, their knowledge is confined to the world. Also, they do not know the world as it truly is; they know only its outward aspect, which is its pleasures and its amusements, and they do not know its inward aspect, which is its harms and its hardships. The second "they" (hum) is mentioned to convey that the heedlessness comes from them, for otherwise the causes of remembrance are present. * * *

As for His saying Most High: ﴿Do they not reflect within themselves?﴾, when the disbelievers expressed denial of God at the denial of God's promise and the absence of failure in it, as He said Most High: ﴿but most people do not know﴾, and denial of the Gathering, as He said Most High: ﴿and they are heedless of the Hereafter﴾, He made clear that the heedlessness and lack of knowledge on their part is by God's decree; otherwise the causes of remembrance are present. Indeed, if they reflected upon their own selves, they would know the oneness of God and would affirm the Gathering. As for oneness, God created them in the best form. Let us mention a part, one part out of a thousand thousand parts, of the goodness of their creation: God Most High created for the human a stomach in which his food is digested so that his limbs may be strengthened by it. It has two openings: one for the entry of food into it, and the other for the exit of food from it. When food enters it, the other opening closes, one part over another, such that not a particle exits from it, nor even by seepage. The retaining organ holds it until it is ripened to a suitable degree, and then it exits from the other opening. God also created beneath the stomach fine, firm veins like a sieve by which a thing is strained; the pure part descends from them to the liver, and the residue pours into an intestine created beneath the stomach, straight and directed towards exit. What enters the liver from the aforementioned veins is called the *māsāriqā* in Hebrew. Hebrew is an Arabic language that has largely been corrupted; it is said of Moses *Mīshā* and of God *Īl*, and other examples. So *māsāriqā* means "the veins/channels," which the liver encloses and ripens with another ripening. Along with the food directed from the stomach to the liver there is an excess of drunk water, so that it may be thinned and flow through the aforementioned fine veins. In the liver it becomes independent of that water, so that water is separated from it and pours from the side of the liver's convex surface to the kidney, together with a small amount of blood by which the kidney and others are nourished. The pure blood exits from the liver through a great vein, then this river branches into rivulets, the rivulets into channels, the channels into streams, and the streams into small outlets, and it reaches the whole body through them. This is one wisdom in the creation of the human being, and it is sufficient for knowing that God is an acting, choosing, powerful, perfect, knowing one whose knowledge encompasses all; and whoever is such must be one, for otherwise he would be incapable when his partner wills the opposite of what he wills.

As for the human's indication of the Gathering: when he reflects upon himself, he sees his powers heading toward cessation and his parts inclining toward dissolution. Thus he has a necessary annihilation. If there were no other life for him, then his being created in this manner for annihilation would be in vain. He indicated this by His saying: ﴿Did you think that We created you in vain?﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 115]. This is evident, because one who does something in vain, even if he perfects and masters it, would be laughed at for it. So when He created him for permanence, and there is no permanence without the meeting, then the Hereafter is necessary.

It has two openings: one for the entry of food into it, and the other for the exit of food from it. When food enters it, the other opening closes, one part over another, such that not a particle exits from it, nor even by seepage. The retaining organ holds it until it is ripened to a suitable degree, and then it exits from the other opening. Hebrew is an Arabic language that has largely been corrupted; it is said of Moses *Mīshā* and of God *Īl*, and other examples. The pure blood exits from the liver through a great vein, then this river branches into rivulets, the rivulets into channels, the channels into streams, and the streams into small outlets, and it reaches the whole body through them. This is one wisdom in the creation of the human being, and it is sufficient for knowing that God is an acting, choosing, powerful, perfect, knowing one whose knowledge encompasses all; and whoever is such must be one, for otherwise he would be incapable when his partner wills the opposite of what he wills.

[Page 89 continued]
greater in wealth and in building, and their wealth and their fortresses did not prevent destruction from them. Know that a person relies on three things: bodily strength, either in himself or in his helpers, since by it is direct action; financial strength, by which one prepares for action; and backing, which he leans on in weakness and lassitude, and this is in fortresses and buildings. So He, exalted, said: they were stronger than them in body and greater than them in wealth, because they ploughed the earth, that is, they tilled it. From this comes "a cow that ploughs the earth" (buqarah tuthiru al-ardh), and it is said that from this the bull was named thawr. You have no tillage, so their wealth was greater, and their building was greater, because their dwellings were lofty and their fortresses were impregnable. The people of Makkah's building was modest. Then these, their messengers came to them with clear proofs, commanded them and forbade them, and when they denied, they were destroyed, so how will you be? His saying: ﴿So Allah would not wrong them﴾ means He did not wrong them by imposing obligations, for the imposition of obligations is noble, and it is not bestowed except upon a noble locus. But they wronged themselves by placing themselves in a base position, which is the worship of idols and the following of Iblis. So Allah, by imposing obligations, placed them in that for which they were created, which is profit, because He, exalted, said: "I created you so that you may gain from Me, not so that I may gain from you." Placing [in any] position for which creation was intended is not wrongdoing. As for them, they placed themselves in positions of loss, though they had been created only for profit, so they were wrongdoers. This statement of ours, although outwardly it resembles the statement of the Mu'tazilah (a rationalist theological school), the intelligent person knows how Ahl al-Sunnah (the People of the Sunnah, the orthodox majority) say it: this placement was by Allah's will and decree, yet it was from them and attributed to them.

Then He, exalted, said: ﴿Then the end of those who did evil was that they denied the signs of Allah and used to mock them.﴾

As He said: ﴿For those who did good is the best [reward]﴾ [Yunus: 26]. As for His saying: ﴿that they denied﴾, it has been said its meaning is "because they denied", that is, their end was that because they denied. And it has been said its meaning is "they did evil and denied", so "denied" is an explanation of "did evil". In this verse there are subtle points.

First: He spoke regarding those who did good: ﴿For those who did good is the best [reward]﴾, and regarding the one who did evil: ﴿Then the end of those who did evil was the worst [reward]﴾. This indicates that Paradise is theirs from the beginning, for al-husna is the name of Paradise and al-suw'a is the name of Hell. When Paradise belongs to them from the beginning, and whoever has something, whatever grows and increases in it is his, because ownership of the root entails ownership of the fruit. So Paradise, from the moment it was created, grows and flourishes for the doers of good. As for those who did evil, the worst, which is Jahannam, is in the end; their destiny is toward it.

Second: He mentioned the increase regarding the doer of good and did not mention an increase regarding the evildoer, because the recompense of an evil deed is an evil deed like it.

Third: He did not mention regarding the doer of good that the best [reward] is his because he affirmed; and He mentioned regarding the evildoer that the worst [reward] is his because he denied. This is because the best [reward] for the doers of good is a bounty, and the one who bestows a bounty, if his bounty were not for a cause, would be more eloquent. As for the worst [reward] for the evildoer, it is justice, and the just, if his punishment were not for a cause, would not be just. So He mentioned the cause in punishment, which is persistence in denial, and did not mention the cause in reward.

* * *

Then He, exalted, said: ﴿Allah originates creation, then repeats it, then to Him you will be returned.﴾

When He mentioned that their end is to the Furnace, and this contained an indication of the return and the gathering, He did not leave it as a claim without proof, so He said: ﴿He originates creation﴾, meaning: whoever created by power and will is not incapable of returning and repeating. ﴿Then to Him you will be returned.﴾ Then He explained what will happen at the time of the return to Him, saying:

﴿And on the day the Hour is established, the criminals will be dumbfounded. And they will have no intercessors from their partners, and they will disbelieve in their partners.﴾

On that day their bankruptcy becomes evident and their dismay is confirmed. Iblas (dismay, despair) is despair together with bewilderment. That is, on the day the Hour is established, the criminal will have a bewildering despair, not the despair that is one of the two comforts. This is because when hope is cut off by despair, if what is hoped for is not a necessity, the one who hopes is relieved from waiting; and if it is a necessity, by its being withheld [from him], his heart is broken with the most severe breaking. Such despair is iblas. To illustrate the condition of the criminal and his dismay, we say: his likeness is that of someone who is in a garden, around him are amusements and pastimes, and he has what he prides himself on and boasts of. Then a truthful person informs him of the coming of an enemy whom no one can repel and no one can turn back. When he comes, he will not let him swallow saliva, and he will leave him no path to escape. So he becomes obliged to take up the path of escape. A child or a madman says to him: "This tree under which you are has properties that repel enemies from whoever is beneath it." That heedless one then turns to enjoying his pleasures, relying on the tree because of the child's words. Then the enemy comes and surrounds him, and the first thing he shows him of the terrors is the uprooting of that tree, so he remains bewildered, despairing and destitute. Likewise the criminal in the abode of this world turns to pursuing pleasures, and the truthful Prophet informed him that Allah will recompense him, and a punishment will come to him that will humiliate him. Then Satan and the soul that commands to evil say to him: "These pieces of wood which are idols are repelling from you every harm, and interceding for you when the senses become dull." So he busies himself with what he is in and persists in his error, until the great catastrophe comes to him. The first thing it shows him is the casting of the idols into the Fire, and he finds no path to escape, and the punishment of burning becomes binding upon him. Then he despairs at that time with the utmost despair, and becomes dumbfounded with the utmost dismay. To this refers His saying, exalted: ﴿And they will have no intercessors from their partners, and they will disbelieve in their partners﴾, meaning: they will disown them on that day.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 30, verses 14–16:

﴿On the Day the Hour is established, on that Day they will be divided.﴾ ﴿As for those who believed and did righteous deeds, they will be in a meadow, made joyful.﴾ ﴿As for those who disbelieved and denied Our signs and the meeting of the Hereafter, they will be brought forth to the punishment.﴾

* * *

Then the Exalted said: ﴿And on the Day the Hour is established, on that Day they will be divided.﴾

Then He explained another matter that will occur on that Day, which is the separation, as the Exalted said in another verse: ﴿And separate yourselves today, O guilty ones.﴾ [Yasin: 59]. So this state appears to follow from the despair (iblas), as if they are first plunged into despair, then distinguished, and one group is placed in Paradise and another group in the Blaze. He repeated His words ﴿And on the Day the Hour is established﴾ because the establishment of the Hour is a tremendous matter, so He repeated it for emphasis in warning. From this, preachers have made a habit of repeating the Day of Resurrection in their sermons to remind people of its terrors.

Then He explained how the division occurs, saying, the Exalted: ﴿As for those who believed and did righteous deeds, they will be in a meadow, made joyful﴾, meaning, in a garden where they will be delighted with every delight. ﴿As for those who disbelieved and denied Our signs and the meeting of the Hereafter, they will be brought forth to the punishment.﴾

That is, they will have no absence from it, and it will not slacken for them, as the Exalted said: ﴿Every time they wish to get out of it from distress, they will be returned into it﴾ [al-Hajj: 22], and He said: ﴿Its punishment will not be lightened for them﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 75], meaning the punishment. In the two verses there are issues containing subtle points:

The first issue: He began with mention of the state of those who believed, although the context is one of mentioning the guilty. That is because the believer receives the reward before the disbeliever receives the punishment, so that it is seen and confirmed that the believer has reached the reward, and this is more painful for the disbeliever. Had the disbeliever been sent into the Fire first, he would have thought that everyone was sharing in the punishment, so He placed that first to increase their pain.

[Page 91]

The second issue: He mentioned righteous deeds for the believer but did not mention evil deeds for the disbeliever. This is because righteous deeds are considered alongside faith, for bare faith is sufficient for salvation without raising the ranks, and the believer does not reach the high rank except by his faith and his righteous deeds. As for the disbeliever, he is in the lower levels merely by his disbelief. So if He had said, "And those who disbelieved and did evil deeds will be brought forth to the punishment," the punishment would apply to whoever commits both. If it is said, "What of one who believes and commits evil deeds, who is not mentioned in either of the two categories?" we say: he has a station between the two stations, not as the Mu'tazila (a theological school) say, but rather he is, in the first case, in the punishment, but not among those constantly brought forth to it; and in the Hereafter he is in the gardens, but not among those utterly delighted. All of this is by the judgment of the promise.

The third issue: He said in the first case, ﴿in a meadow﴾ in indefinite form, and in the other case, ﴿in the punishment﴾ in definite form, to magnify the meadow through indefiniteness, as one says: "So-and-so has wealth and standing," meaning abundant and great.

The fourth issue: In the first case He said ﴿made joyful﴾ in verbal form, and did not say "made joyful" in the nominal form (mahbur). In the other case He said ﴿brought forth﴾ in nominal form (muhdarun), and did not say "they will be brought forth" (yuhdarun). This is because the verbal form indicates renewal, while the nominal form does not indicate it. So His words ﴿made joyful﴾ mean that there comes to them every hour a matter by which they are delighted. As for the disbelievers, when they enter the punishment they remain in it, brought forth.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 30, verses 17–19 (part 1 of 2):

Then God the Exalted said: ﴿So glorify God when you enter the evening and when you enter the morning﴾ ﴿And to Him belongs praise in the heavens and the earth, and at nightfall and when you reach noon﴾ ﴿He brings the living out of the dead, and brings the dead out of the living, and brings the earth to life after its death. And thus you will be brought forth﴾.

When God the Exalted had shown His greatness at the beginning, with His words ﴿God did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them except with truth﴾, and His greatness at the end, which is the time when the Hour comes and people are divided into two groups, with Him judging some to Paradise without concern, and others to the Fire without concern, He commanded them to declare Him free of every imperfection and to praise Him in every state, saying: ﴿So glorify God﴾, meaning: glorify God with glorification (tasbih). In this verse there are several issues.

The first issue concerns the meaning and the wording of *subhana Allah* (glory be to God). As for its wording, *subhan* is a noun that stands for the verbal noun, which is *tasbih* (glorification). *Tasbih* has been named *subhan* and made a proper name for it. As for its meaning, some exegetes said: it means prayer, that is, pray, and they mentioned that it refers to the five daily prayers. Others said it means *tanzih* (declaring God free of imperfection), that is, declare Him free of attributes of deficiency and describe Him with attributes of perfection. This is stronger, and adopting it is preferable, because it includes the first meaning. This is because the *tanzih* commanded here encompasses *tanzih* by the heart, which is firm belief, and by the tongue along with that, which is good remembrance, and by the limbs together with both of these, which is righteous action. The first is the root, the second is the fruit of the first, and the third is the fruit of the second. This is because when a person believes something, it appears from his heart upon his tongue, and when he speaks, the truth of his speech appears in his states and actions. The tongue is the interpreter of the heart, and the limbs are the proof of the tongue. However, prayer is the best of the deeds of the limbs, and it includes remembrance with the tongue and intention with the heart, and in reality it is *tanzih*. So when He says "declare Me free", this is one kind of *tanzih*, and a general command is not restricted to one kind over another, so it must be understood as applying to everything that is *tanzih*, and thus this is also a command to pray. Furthermore, our statement fits what came before. This is because when God the Exalted showed that the supreme station and the complete reward belong to those who believe and do righteous deeds, saying: ﴿As for those who believed and did righteous deeds, they will be in a garden, made joyful﴾, He said: If you know that this station belongs to those who believe and do righteous deeds, and faith is *tanzih* by the heart and *tawhid* (affirmation of God's oneness) by the tongue, and righteous action is the use of the limbs, and all of these are declarations of God's freedom from imperfection and praises, then "glorify God" means: do that which leads to joy in the gardens and to presence at the watering-places.

* * *

The second issue: God singled out certain times for the command to glorify Him. This is because the best of deeds is the most constant of them. The best of the angels are constantly devoted to glorification, as God the Exalted said: ﴿They glorify Him night and day, never tiring﴾ [al-Anbiya: 20]. A human being, as long as he is in this world, cannot devote all his times to glorification, because he needs food, drink, obtaining what is eaten and drunk, clothing and mounts. So God the Exalted pointed to times in which, if the servant glorifies God, it is as though he has not tired. These times are the beginning, the end, and the middle: the beginning of the day, its end, and its middle. So He commanded glorification at the beginning and middle of the night, and did not command glorification at the end of the night, because sleep predominates in it, and God has favored His servants with the rest of sleep, as He said: ﴿And among His signs is your sleep at night﴾ [al-Rum: 23]. When a person prays two units at the beginning of the day, which are two rak'ahs, it is counted for him as devoting two hours to glorification. Then when he prays four rak'ahs at the time of Zuhr, it is counted for him as devoting four more hours, making six hours. When he prays four at the end of the day, which is 'Asr, four more are counted for him, making ten hours. Then when he prays Maghrib and 'Isha' with seven more rak'ahs, he attains the devotion of seventeen hours to glorification. There remain seven hours of the night and day, which are between midnight and its two-thirds. This is because two-thirds of the night is eight hours and half of it is six hours, and between them is seven. This amount, if a person sleeps during it, would be a great deal, and God pointed to it with His words: ﴿Stand [in prayer] by night, except for a little﴾ ﴿half of it, or reduce it a little﴾ ﴿or add to it﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 2–4]. The addition of a little to half is one hour, so it becomes seven hours devoted to sleep. The one who sleeps has the pen lifted from him, so God says: My servant has devoted all the times of his obligation to glorifying Me. So there remains for you, O angels, no superiority over them on the basis of exclusivity, which you claimed by your words: ﴿While we glorify You with Your praise and sanctify You﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30]. Rather, they are like you, and their station is like your station in the highest 'Illiyyin.

Know that in the appointing of the prayer to its times, in the number of its rak'ahs, and in the variation of its forms, there is profound wisdom. As for the number of rak'ahs, it is based on what has preceded: that a human being is awake for seventeen hours, so He obligated seventeen rak'ahs upon him. As for the school of Abu Hanifa (may God have mercy on him), who held that the witr prayer is obligatory as three rak'ahs, and this is closer to piety, we say it is derived from the fact that a human being should minimize his sleep, so that he sleeps only a third of the night, derived from God's words: ﴿Indeed your Lord knows that you stand [in prayer] less than two-thirds of the night, or half of it, or a third of it﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 20]. It is understood from this that standing for two-thirds of the night is commendable, recommended and strongly encouraged. For this reason He said after it: ﴿He knew that you would not be able to keep count of it, so He turned to you [in mercy]﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 20], and it is mentioned with the word "turning" (tawbah). If this is the case, a person is awake for twenty hours, so he is commanded twenty rak'ahs. As for the Prophet (peace be upon him), since it was part of his nature never to sleep at all, as he said: "My eyes sleep but my heart does not sleep," the whole night was made for him like the day, and tahajjud was added for him and he was commanded to perform it. To this God pointed in His words: ﴿And part of the night, prostrate to Him and glorify Him throughout a long night﴾ [al-Insan: 26], meaning: the whole night is for you for glorification. So he became, in twenty-four hours, one who glorifies, and thus one of those who do not tire even for the blink of an eye. As for the times of the prayers, what has been said before also applies: that the beginning, the end, and the middle are what is taken into account. So He prescribed glorification at the beginning and end of the day. As for the night, He took its beginning and middle into account, just as He took the beginning and middle of the day into account. This is because the time of Zuhr is midday, and the time of 'Isha' is midnight. This is because we have explained that the night which is taken into account is the amount during which a person is awake, which is five hours. So its time was placed at the middle of this amount, which is the third hour of the night. As for Abu Hanifa, since he saw the obligation of witr, the time of sleep for him was four hours and the time of wakefulness at night was eight hours, and he delayed the time of 'Isha' al-Akhirah to the fourth and fifth hours, so that it would be in the middle of the night that is taken into account, just as Zuhr is in the middle of the day. As for the Prophet (peace be upon him), since his night was like day and his sleep was alertness, he said: "Were it not that I would burden my community, I would command them to use the miswak and to delay 'Isha' until midnight," so that the four would be at midnight just as the four are at midday. As for the detail, what appears to me is that the day is twelve temporal hours, and the prayers performed in it are ten rak'ahs, so there remain for the one who is obligated two rak'ahs, which he performs at the beginning of the night, and he performs one rak'ah of the night prayer, so that the beginning of the night is with glorification just as the beginning of the day was with glorification. Since what is performed of the day's glorification at its beginning is two rak'ahs, what is performed of the night's glorification at its beginning is one rak'ah. This is because the glorification of the day is long, about twice the glorification of the night, since what is performed in the day is ten, and what is performed in the night of the night's glorification is five.

The third issue concerns the virtue of *al-sabhala* (saying subhan Allah) and *al-hamdala* (saying al-hamdu lillah) in the evening and morning. Let us mention it from the standpoint of transmission (naql) and reason ('aql). As for transmission, the pious shaykh, the memorizer of hadith, the master 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Abd Allah ibn 'Ulwan informed me in Aleppo, with a chain of narration (isnad) traced back: "From the Prophet (peace be upon him) that he said to one of his companions: 'Are you unable to gain a thousand good deeds at the time of sleep?' He hesitated, so the Prophet (peace be upon him) said: 'Say: Glory be to God, praise be to God, and God is greatest, one hundred times, and a thousand good deeds will be written for you by them.'" I also heard him say, may God have mercy on him, with a continuous chain: "Whoever says after every obligatory prayer ten times 'Glory be to God' and ten times 'God is greatest' will enter Paradise." As for reason, God the Exalted has attributes that are necessary to Him, not from His action, and attributes that are established for Him from His action. As for the first, they are attributes of perfection and majesty, the opposite of which is deficiency. So when the responsible person recognizes God as one who cannot be unaware of anything, because He is knowing of everything, he has declared Him free of ignorance and described Him by its opposite. When he knows Him as one who cannot be incapable of anything, because He is capable of everything, he has declared Him free of incapacity. When he knows that nothing moves in His dominion except what He wills, because He wills every existing thing, he has described Him and declared Him free. When it becomes clear to him that annihilation cannot happen to Him, because He is necessarily everlasting, he has declared Him free. When it becomes evident to him that non-existence cannot precede Him, because He is characterized by eternity, he has declared Him free. When it appears to him that He cannot be an accident or a body in a place, because He is necessary, free of the directions of possibility, he has declared Him free.

However, His negative and relational attributes cannot be counted by any counter, even if one were to occupy himself with them, he would spend his whole life on them and not grasp their reality. If someone says, present in his heart "Glory be to God," attentive to what he says, meaning that he declares Him free of every deficiency, then his saying of the glorification in this general way stands in place of saying it in detail. Yet there is no doubt that whoever recites the glorification for each thing separately which is impossible for God has recited what the lifetimes cannot contain. Then God says: This servant has glorified Me throughout his life and the duration of his existence, so I will reward him by purifying him from every sin, adorning him with robes of honor, and lodging him in the abode of permanence for a period without end. Just as the servant declares God free at the beginning of the day, at its end, and in its middle, so God the Exalted purifies him at its beginning, which is his worldly life, at its end, which is his afterlife, and in its middle, which is his state while he is in his grave until the time of his resurrection, and that is its meaning.

As for the second, which are the attributes of action, when a human being looks at God's creation of the heavens, he knows that it is a blessing and a favor, so he says: "Praise be to God." When he sees the sun rising in them, he knows that it is a blessing and a favor.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 30, verses 17–19 (part 2 of 2):

He says, "Praise be to God," and likewise the moon, every star, the earth, every plant and every animal says, "Praise be to God." Then, when a person is absorbed in the attributes of God, his intellect may call him to reflect upon God the Exalted after reflecting upon the signs of God. So whatever falls into his intellect of the reality of Him, he should say "God is greater" than what he has grasped; for the things grasped and the aspects of grasping have no end. If he wishes to say, in detail, "God is greater than this which I have grasped from this aspect, and greater than what I have grasped from that aspect, and greater than what I have grasped from another aspect," his lifetime would be spent, and he would not be able to grasp all the aspects by which the one who supposes he grasps God through that aspect thinks he grasps Him. So when he says to himself "God is greater," meaning greater than everything I imagine by the power of my intellect and the capacity of my perception, he is deeply immersed in gnosis, and to this refers the saying:

"Incapacity to attain the attaining is itself attainment."

So the words of the awakened speaker, "Glory be to God, praise be to God, and God is greater," produce these benefits; but its condition is that it be words of consequence, which come from the depth of the heart, not those which come from the tip of the tongue.

The fourth issue: His saying ﴿and in the evening﴾ is conjoined to "time," meaning: glorify Him when you reach the evening, when you reach the morning, and in the evening. Therefore they must praise God when they glorify Him. This is like His saying: ﴿They consider it a favour to you that they have embraced Islam. Most of them said: He brings forth the hen from the egg and the egg from the hen; likewise the animal from the sperm-drop and the sperm-drop from the animal. Others said: the believer from the disbeliever and the disbeliever from the believer. It is possible to say that what is meant is: ﴿He brings forth the living from the dead﴾, i.e., the wakeful from the sleeper and the sleeper from the wakeful, and this would be mentioned as an illustration, i.e., the giving of life to the dead in his sight, and the causing of death to the living, like the waking of the sleeper and the putting to sleep of the awake.

Then the Exalted said: ﴿And He brings the earth to life after its death; and so you will be brought forth﴾. This is because the elements (al-'anasir) are further [from life] than compounds (al-murakkabat), since a compound, by its composition, is closer in rank to the animal. Among the elements, dust is the furthest, because water has in it clarity, moisture and motion, and all of these are of the nature of spirits. Fire is closer, because it is like the innate heat (al-hararah al-ghariziyyah), which brings things to maturity, gathers them, and separates them.

Then come the compounds. The first of their levels is the mineral (al-ma'dan), for it is mixed. It has levels, the highest of which is gold, which is close to the lowest level of plants, namely the plant that grows in the ground and does not stand out or rise up. Then come the plants, and the highest of their levels is the level of trees that accept growth in size, and whose fruit contains a seed from which a tree of the same kind is produced, as an egg is produced from a hen and a hen from an egg. This is close to the lowest level of animals, namely the level of insects (al-hasharat), which do not have flowing blood and are not conduits of great benefits as plants are. Then comes the animal, and the highest of its levels is close to the level of man, for livestock, especially the horse, resemble the porter, the carrier and the runner. Then comes man. The highest level of man is close to the level of the angels who glorify God and praise Him. So God, who created a living being from that which is furthest from the level of the living, is in the highest of levels, and is not but exalted above incapacity and ignorance, and praise is due to Him for bestowing life, and He has perfect power and the unhindered execution of His will, so that both origination and return are possible from Him.

In the verse there are two subtle points.

The first: His saying ﴿then﴾ (idha), which is for suddenness, as one says, "I went out, and behold (fa-idha), a lion is at the door." This indicates that God created him from dust by His saying "Be!" and he came to be, not that he became a mineral, then a plant, then an animal, then a human. This points to a rational (hukmiyyah) question, namely that God first creates a human, and makes him aware that he will live as an animal, a growing thing, and other things, and not that He first created an animal and then made it a human. So the creation of the species is the primary intention, and then the species contain within them the genera, by that first will. God has made the final level in the thing, which is far from it, an end without transition from one level to another of the levels we have mentioned.

The second subtle point: His saying ﴿human beings (bashar)﴾ indicates the faculty of perception, because the bashar is called bashar by his skin, not by his movement, for other animals are also like this. His saying ﴿spreading out﴾ indicates the faculty of motion. Both of these from dust is wondrous. As for perception, it is due to its density and immobility; as for motion, it is due to its heaviness and inertness. And His saying ﴿spreading out﴾ indicates that the wonder is not specific to the creation of man from dust, but the creation of the animal that spreads out from the still dust is wondrous, let alone the creation of human beings.

[p. 96]

In the verse there are issues.

The first issue: God created Adam from dust and created us from him, so how does He say ﴿He created you from dust﴾? We say the answer to this is from two aspects.

One of them: it has been said that the meaning of His saying ﴿He created you﴾ is that He created your origin.

The second: We say that every human being is created from dust. As for Adam, it is clear. As for us, it is because we were created from a drop (nutfah), and the drop comes from the good nourishment which is, potentially, some of the limbs. Nourishment is either from the flesh of animals, their milk, and their fat, or from plants. Animals also have a nourishment which is plants, but plants come from dust, for a grain of wheat or the stone of a fruit does not become a tree except by means of dust, and parts of water join with it, so that the plant becomes such that it nourishes.

The second issue: God says in another place: ﴿He created a human from water﴾ [al-Furqan: 54], and He says: ﴿from a fluid of despised water﴾ [al-Sajdah: 8]. Here He says: ﴿from dust﴾. So how is this to be reconciled? We say: As for the first answer, the question disappears, for what is meant by it is Adam.

As for the second answer, we say: here He mentioned what is the first origin, and in that other place He mentioned what is the second origin, because that dust which became nourishment turns into a fluid, which is the seminal fluid (al-mani), then it coagulates and, by God's creation, becomes a human from it. Or we say: the human has two apparent origins, water and dust, for dust does not produce growth except by water. So in the plant, which is the origin of human nourishment, there is dust and water. If dust is taken as the origin and water as that which gathers its scattered parts, then the matter is so. If the origin is taken to be water and dust, in order to hold its moist parts from flowing, then the matter is also so. If someone says: God knows everything, so He knows what the origin truly is of the two, and for us the matter is ambiguous, and either this or that is possible. If the origin is dust, then how does He say ﴿from water a human﴾? And if it is water, how does He say ﴿He created you from dust﴾? And if both are the two origins, why does He not say "He created you from both of them"? We say: In this there is a subtle point, namely that dust being an origin and water being an origin, and that water is not so by its own essence, but by the making of God, exalted is He. For God, considering His power, could have created the human first, then annihilated him so that dust resulted from him, then dissolved him so that water resulted from him. But wisdom required that the deficient be a means to the complete, not that the complete be a means to the deficient. So He created dust and water first, and made them two origins for the one who is more complete than them, indeed for the one who is the most complete of every existent, which is the human. If their being two origins is not an inherent matter for them, but by the making of a maker, then at one time He made dust the origin, and at another time water, so that it would be known that it is by His will and choice. If He wills, He makes this the origin; if He wills, He makes that the origin; and if He wills, He makes both of them origins.

The third issue: The philosophers (al-hukama') have said that man is composed of the four elements, which are earth, water, air and fire. They said: earth is in him for its stability, water for its cohesion, for dust crumbles quickly; air for its independence, like an inflated waterskin which stands up by the air, and without it there would be neither independence nor erectness in it; and fire for ripening and for the joining together of these things. So is this correct or not? If it is correct, how did He consider only two of them, and did not say in another place that He created you from fire or from wind? We say: As for their statement, there is no corruption in it from the standpoint of the Law, so we do not dispute with them about it, unless they say that it is so by nature. As for if they say that God, by His wisdom, created the human from these things, then we do not dispute with them about it. As for the verses, we say that what you have mentioned does not contradict this, for you have made air for independence and fire for ripening, and these two come after the mixing of water with dust. So the origin that is present is only the first two, and for this reason He singled them out. And also, because what is perceived of the elements in general is dust and water, especially since their presence in man is evident to everyone, so He singled out the evident and perceptible by mention.

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And among His signs is that He created for you spouses from among yourselves, that you may find tranquility in them; and He placed between you affection and mercy. Indeed in that are signs for a people who give thought.﴾

When Allah explained the creation of man, He explained that when He created man, and since he was not among the things that endure and last for long periods, He preserved his species through individuals and made him such that he reproduces. So when the father dies, the son takes his place, lest the loss of the one cause a breach in the building that cannot be closed. In the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: His saying ﴿He created for you﴾ is evidence that women were created like the animals, the plants and other benefits, as Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿He created for you all that is in the earth﴾ [al-Baqarah: 29]. This implies that they were not created for worship and obligation. So we say: the creation of women is among the blessings upon us, and their creation for us and their being obligated serve to complete the blessing upon us, not to direct obligation toward them in the way it is directed toward us. This is in terms of transmission (naql), ruling (hukm) and meaning (ma'na). As for transmission, this and other evidence. As for ruling, women are not charged with many obligations as men are. As for meaning, women are weak in constitution and light-minded, so they resemble a child; but the child is not charged, so it would be fitting that women not be qualified for obligation. Yet the blessing upon us would not be complete except through their being charged, so that each of them fears punishment, submits to the husband, and refrains from what is forbidden. Were it not so, corruption would appear.

The second issue: His saying ﴿from among yourselves﴾. Some said: what is meant is that Hawwa' (Eve) was created from the body of Adam. The correct view is that what is meant is from among your kind (jins), as Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿There has certainly come to you a Messenger from among yourselves﴾ [al-Tawbah: 128]. This is supported by His saying ﴿that you may find tranquility in them﴾, meaning that two living, differing kinds do not find tranquility in one another, i.e., one's self does not settle with the other and one's heart does not incline to it.

The third issue: It is said "sakana ilayhi" (he found tranquility toward him) for the tranquility of the heart, and "sakana 'indahu" (he dwelt with him) for physical rest; because the word 'inda (with/at) is used for the place of physical location, which is for bodies, while ila (toward) denotes the endpoint, and it is for hearts.

The fourth issue: His saying ﴿and He placed between you affection and mercy﴾. Concerning it there are several views. Some said: affection is through intercourse and mercy is toward the child, relying on His saying: ﴿a mention of the mercy of your Lord toward His servant Zakariyya﴾ [Maryam: 2]. Others said: affection is in the state of one's own need, and mercy is in the state of the need of one's companion for him. This is because a person loves, for example, his child; yet when he sees his enemy in a state of severe hunger and pain, he may take from his child and use it to relieve that condition. That is not due to the cause of love, but to the cause of mercy. It may also be said that He earlier mentioned two matters: one, that the spouse is of one's own kind; and two, what the kinship leads to, which is tranquility toward it. So kinship produces tranquility. Here He mentioned two matters: one leads to the other, so affection comes first, then it leads to mercy. For this reason, a wife may leave the object of desire through old age or sickness while the husband's care for her remains, and vice versa. His saying ﴿Indeed in that﴾ may be taken to mean: the intended meaning is that in the creation of spouses there are signs; and it may also be taken to mean that in the placing of affection between them there are signs.

As for the first: it requires reflection, because the creation of man from two parents indicates perfect power, the executing of will, and comprehensive knowledge, for whoever reflects, even on the emergence of the child from the mother's womb. For were that coming-forth from other than Allah, it would lead to the destruction of the mother and the destruction of the child as well; for if the child were drawn out from a narrow place without the help of Allah, it would die.

As for the second: it is likewise, because a person finds between the two spouses a mutual compassion that he does not find between blood relatives. That is not by mere desire, for desire may cease while mercy remains. So it is from Allah; for if between them there were only desire, and anger which frequently occurs and nullifies desire, and desire is not lasting in itself, then every hour there would be separation and divorce between them. Thus the mercy by which a person repels hardships from the sanctity of his household is from the presence of Allah, and this is known only through reflection.

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And among His signs is the creation of the heavens and the earth, and the difference of your languages and your colors. Indeed in that are signs for those who know.﴾

When He had shown the proofs drawn from the self (anfus), He mentioned the proofs drawn from the horizons (afaq). The most evident of these is the creation of the heavens and the earth. Some of the disbelievers say, regarding the creation of humans and other compounds, that it is due to the qualities found in the elements (al-'anasir) and to the motions found in the heavens and to the conjunctions (al-ittisalat) found in them. So when it is said to him: "Then the heavens and the earth did not come about through the mixing of the elements or the conjunctions of the stars," he has no choice but to say that this is by the power and will of Allah.

Then, when He had pointed to the proofs of the self and the horizons, He mentioned what belongs to the attributes of the self: the difference among human colors. Indeed one of them, despite the multitude of their number and the smallness of the size of their cheeks and forms, is not confused with another, whereas the heavens, despite their greatness and the fewness of their number, are similar in form.

The second: the difference of their speech. Indeed two Arabs who are brothers, when they speak in one language, one of them is recognized from the other, to the point that someone who is hidden from them and cannot see them says, "This is the voice of so-and-so, and this is the voice of the other so-and-so." In this there is profound wisdom. That is because a person needs to distinguish between individuals, in order to know the one who has a right from others, and the enemy from the friend, so that he may guard himself before the enemy reaches him, and turn toward the friend before the opportunity of turning to him is lost. This may be by sight, so He created the difference of forms; and it may be by hearing, so He created the difference of voices. As for touch, smell and taste, they do not serve any benefit in recognizing the enemy and the friend, so distinction is not achieved by them. Some people have said: the intended meaning is the difference of languages, such as Arabic, Persian, Roman and others; but the first is more correct.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed in that are signs for those who know.﴾ Since the creation of the heavens and the earth does not admit of the remote possibilities which the proponents of natures (ashab al-taba'i') put forward, and the difference of colors is likewise, and the difference of voices is likewise, He said: ﴿for those who know﴾, for the generality of knowledge concerning that.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 30, verse 23:

Then the Exalted said: ﴿And among His signs is your sleep by night and by day, and your seeking of His bounty. Indeed in that are signs for a people who listen.﴾

Page 99
When He mentioned some of the necessary accidents, namely the variation of accidents that are separable (mufariqah), among which is sleep by night and movement seeking provision by day, He mentioned two of the necessary ones and two of the separable ones. In the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: His saying: ﴿your sleep by night and by day﴾. It has been said that He meant by it sleep at night and sleep during the day, which is the qaylulah (afternoon nap). Then He said: ﴿and your seeking﴾, meaning within both of them, for a person often earns in the night. It has also been said that He meant: your sleep at night and your seeking by day, so He wrapped one part with the other. This is indicated by other verses, among them the words of the Exalted: ﴿And We made the sign of the day to be seeing, that you might seek bounty﴾ [al-Isra: 12], and His saying: ﴿And We made the night a covering, and We made the day for livelihood﴾ [al-Naba: 10–11]. The construction would then be: "And among His signs is your sleep and your seeking, by night and by day, of His bounty." He delayed the seeking and joined it in wording to the verb, indicating that the servant should not regard provision as coming from his own earning and cleverness, but should regard all of that as from the bounty of his Lord. For this reason He joined seeking with bounty in many places, among them the words of the Exalted: ﴿And when the prayer is concluded, disperse in the land and seek of the bounty of Allah﴾ [al-Jumu'ah: 10], and His saying: ﴿that you may seek of His bounty﴾ [al-Nahl: 14].

The third issue: He said: ﴿signs for a people who listen﴾, and He said earlier: ﴿for a people who reflect﴾, and He said: ﴿for those of knowledge﴾. We say: sleep by night and seeking of His bounty, the ignorant or heedless person may think that these are among the things required by the nature of living beings, so it is not evident to everyone that they are among the blessings of Allah. Therefore He did not say "signs for those of knowledge." Also, the first two matters, namely the variation of tongues and colours, are among the necessary things, whereas sleep and seeking are among the separable matters. Looking at the latter two does not last, since they cease at some times, whereas the variation of tongues and colours does not, for they endure as long as the human being endures. So He made those two general signs. As for His saying: ﴿for a people who reflect﴾, know that among things there is what is known without reflection, and among them what is sufficed by mere thought, and among them what does not emerge by thought alone but requires a standpoint on which one is made to stand and a guide who directs one to it, so that when one hears it from that guide, one understands it. And among them what some people need, for its comprehension, sensible examples, such as geometric figures. But the creation of pairs does not occur to anyone by nature as a sign, except to one whose thought is frozen and whose remembrance is dormant; when he reflects he knows that this creation is a sign. As for sleep and seeking, it often occurs to many that they are acts of the servants, and they may need a guide without reflection. So He said: ﴿for a people who listen﴾, and they give their attention to the words of the guide.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 30, verses 24–25:

Then God Most High said: ﴿And among His signs is that He shows you the lightning, as a fear and a hope, and sends down water from the sky, and by it revives the earth after its death. Indeed in that are signs for a people who use their reason.﴾

When He mentioned the accidents (al-'aradiyyat) of the selves that are necessary (al-lazima) and those that are separable (al-mufaraqa), He mentioned the accidents of the horizons, saying: ﴿He shows you the lightning, as a fear and a hope, and sends down from the sky﴾. Regarding the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: When He presented the proofs from the selves here, He placed first the accidents of the selves and delayed the accidents of the horizons, just as He delayed the proofs from the horizons with His saying: ﴿And among His signs is the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾.

The second issue: He placed the necessary attributes of the selves before the separable accidents, since He first mentioned the difference of tongues and colours, then the sleep and the seeking (of provision). He placed the separable accidents of the horizons before the necessary attributes, since He said: ﴿He shows you the lightning, as a fear and a hope, and sends down﴾. This is because man's state changes, and accidents are not far from him, whereas necessary attributes in him are close. As for the heavens and the earth, they change little, so accidents in them are more strange than necessary attributes. Thus He placed what is more wondrous, because it is more fitting for it to be a sign. Let us clarify this further: man's state changes with age, with youth and old age, with health and sickness; yet he has a voice by which he is recognized which does not change, and a colour that distinguishes him from others. He changes in states while that does not change, and this is a wondrous sign. The sky and the earth are fixed and do not change; then, at certain times, heavy rains and terrifying lightning are seen, while the sky remains as it was and the earth likewise. So this is a sign indicating a free-choosing agent (fa'il mukhtar) who makes one matter continue while the place changes, and removes another matter while the place remains fixed.

The third issue: Just as He placed the sky before the earth, He placed what comes from the sky, namely the lightning and the rain, before what comes from the earth, namely the growing of plants and the giving of life.

The fourth issue: Just as there are benefits in the sending down of rain and the growth of trees, so too there is benefit in the lightning and thunder preceding the rain. This is because when lightning appears, whoever is not under shelter fears being soaked and prepares for it; whoever has a cistern or a reservoir needs water; whoever has crops arranges the channels of water. Also, the Arabs who dwell in the desert would not know the grassy lands unless they had seen the lightning flashing from one side rather than another. Know that the benefits of lightning, even if they are not apparent to those who dwell in towns, are apparent to the nomads. For this reason He made the lightning's preceding the sending down of water from the sky a blessing and a sign. As for its being a sign, it is evident: in the cloud there is nothing but water and air, yet fire comes out of it so that it burns mountains, which is extremely strange. Therefore there must be a creator, and He is God.

The philosophers said: the cloud has density and subtlety in comparison with air and water. Air is subtler than it, and water is denser. When a strong wind blows and tears through the cloud violently, the sound of thunder arises, and fire comes out of it, like a body touching another body violently. This is like the fire that comes out when a stone strikes iron.

If someone says: the stone and the iron are solid bodies, while the cloud and the wind are moist bodies. They reply: but the movement of a human hand is weak, while the movement of the wind is strong, uprooting trees. We say to them: lightning and thunder are two originated things (hadithan) that must have a cause, and it has been established by proof that every originated thing is from God; therefore they are from God. Then we say: suppose the matter is as you say; the blowing of that strong wind is among the wondrous originated events, and it must have a cause that ends at the Necessary Existent (wajib al-wujud). So it is a sign for the intelligent person of God's power, however you suppose it.

The fifth issue: He said here: ﴿for a people who use their reason﴾. Since the birth of a child from its parent is an ordinary, regular matter with little variation, the common delusions could come to think that this is by nature (al-tab'), because the regular is closer to nature than the varied. But lightning and rain are not a regular matter that never fails, since they fall in one land and not another, at one time and not another, sometimes strong and sometimes weak. Therefore it is more evident to reason as an indication of a free-choosing agent. So He said: it is a sign for whoever has reason, if he does not reflect with complete reflection.

* *

Then God Most High said: ﴿And among His signs is that the heaven and the earth stand by His command. Then, when He calls you with a single call from the earth, behold, you will come forth.﴾

When He mentioned some of the accidents of the heaven and the earth, He mentioned some of their necessary attributes, namely their standing. For the earth, because of its heaviness, a person marvels at its standing still and not falling. And the heaven: a person marvels at its height and its stability without pillars. This is among the necessary attributes, for the earth does not leave its place in which it is, and the heaven likewise does not leave its place in which it is. If it is said that they move in their place like a millstone, yet the sane have agreed that they do not leave their place. This is a clear sign, because their being in the place they are in and upon the place they are upon is among the possible matters, while their being in other than that place is also possible. So it would be possible for them to leave it. Since they did not leave, this is a preference of the possible over its alternative, and that cannot occur except by a free-choosing agent.

The philosophers said: the earth's being in the place it is in is natural to it, because it is the heaviest of things, and the heavy seeks the centre, while the light seeks the surrounding sphere. As for the heaven, its being in its place, if it has a place, is by its essence; so its standing in them is by its own nature. We say: it has been said many times before that the doctrine of nature is false. What we add here is that you agreed with us that what is permissible for one of two like things is permissible for the other like thing. But the concave of the sphere does not differ from its convex in nature, so it is permissible for its concave to occur in the place of its convex, and this is by departure and cessation. Thus cessation from a place is possible, especially for the lowest heaven, since by your own school it is bounded by directions too. The earth also could undergo circular motion as you say of the heaven. So its non-existence and its stillness are only by a free-choosing agent.

Issues concerning the verse:

The first issue: God mentioned two matters from each category. From the selves He mentioned: ﴿He created for you﴾, deriving evidence from the creation of the pair. From the horizons He mentioned the heaven and the earth in His saying: ﴿the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾. From the necessary attributes of man: the difference of tongues and colours; from his separable accidents: sleep and seeking. From the accidents of the horizons: lightning and rain; from their necessary attributes: the standing of the heaven and the standing of the earth. This is because one (proof) suffices for an affirmation of the truth, while the second yields conjecture, and another's statement yields its confirmation. For this reason Abraham, peace be upon him, said: ﴿Yes, but that my heart may be at rest﴾ [al-Baqara 2:260].

The second issue: His saying ﴿by His command﴾ means: by His word, "Be" (qawman), or by His will for their standing. This is because, according to the Mu'tazila, command coincides with will, while according to us it is not so. Yet the dispute concerns the command that is for obligation (al-taklif), not the command that is for origination (al-takwin). For we do not dispute with them that His saying "Be" (kun) and "Be, O fire, cool" ﴿Be cool, O fire﴾ [al-Anbiya' 21:69] coincides with the will.

The third issue: He said here ﴿And among His signs is that [it] stands﴾, and before it He said ﴿And among His signs is that He shows you﴾, and He did not say "that He shows you". Although some exegetes said that "an" (that) is implied there, meaning "from His signs (that He shows you)", so that it becomes like a verbal noun with "an". This is because standing, since it does not change, He turned the verb with "an" away from the future tense and made it a verbal noun, since the future tense indicates renewal. As for lightning, since it is among matters that renew at one time and not another, He mentioned it with the future-tense form and did not attach any verbal particles to it.

The fourth issue: He mentioned six proofs, and in four of them He said ﴿Indeed in that are signs﴾. He did not say it for the first, which is His saying ﴿And among His signs is that He created you from dust﴾, nor for the other, which is His saying ﴿And among His signs is that the heaven and the earth stand﴾. As for the first, this is because His saying after it ﴿And among His signs is that He created for you﴾ is also a proof from the selves; the creation of the selves and the creation of the spouses are from one category, as we explained, except that He mentioned two matters from each category for the sake of affirmation through repetition. So when He said ﴿Indeed in that are signs﴾, it refers back to both. As for the standing of the heaven and the earth, we say: regarding the heavenly signs He mentioned that they are signs for those who know, and for a people who use reason, because of their manifestness. Since at the beginning of the matter it is manifest, at the end of the matter, after the enumeration of proofs, it becomes even more manifest. So He did not distinguish anyone from anyone in that, and He mentioned what it signifies, which is His power over the resurrection, and He said: ﴿Then, when He calls you with a single call from the earth, behold, you will come forth.﴾ There are issues concerning this:

The first issue: What is the reason for the conjunction "then" (thumma), and to what does "then" attach? We say its meaning, and God knows best, is: when He has shown you the perfection of His power through these signs, after that He informs you and makes you know that when He says to the decayed bones, "Come forth from the graves," they come forth alive.

The second issue: The speaker's saying "So-and-so called so-and-so from the mountain" may mean that the calling is from the mountain, as the speaker says, "O so-and-so, ascend to the mountain," so it is said, "He called him from the mountain." It may also mean that the one called is called from the mountain, as the speaker says, "O so-and-so, come down from the mountain," so it is said, "He called him from the mountain." It is not hidden from the intelligent that calling does not come from the earth if the caller is God. So the one called is called from the earth, meaning: you are in the earth, and He calls you from it, and you come forth.

The third issue: His saying ﴿behold [idha]﴾: we have explained that it is for sudden occurrence (lil-mufaja'a), meaning that it happens by "Be," and it is.

The fourth issue: He said here ﴿behold, you will come forth﴾, and in the creation of man at first He said: ﴿then, behold, you are humans spreading out﴾ [al-Rum 30:20]. We say: there, there is creation, measuring, gradualness, and delay until the dust becomes receptive to life, and then He breathes into it His spirit, and behold, it is a human being. But in the resurrection there is no gradualness or delay; rather there is a call and a coming forth. Therefore He did not say "then" here.
