Regarding the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: When He presented the proofs from the selves here, He placed first the accidents of the selves and delayed the accidents of the horizons, just as He delayed the proofs from the horizons with His saying: ﴿And among His signs is the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾.

The second issue: He placed the necessary attributes of the selves before the separable accidents, since He first mentioned the difference of tongues and colours, then the sleep and the seeking (of provision). He placed the separable accidents of the horizons before the necessary attributes, since He said: ﴿He shows you the lightning, as a fear and a hope, and sends down﴾. This is because man's state changes, and accidents are not far from him, whereas necessary attributes in him are close. As for the heavens and the earth, they change little, so accidents in them are more strange than necessary attributes. Thus He placed what is more wondrous, because it is more fitting for it to be a sign. Let us clarify this further: man's state changes with age, with youth and old age, with health and sickness; yet he has a voice by which he is recognized which does not change, and a colour that distinguishes him from others. He changes in states while that does not change, and this is a wondrous sign. The sky and the earth are fixed and do not change; then, at certain times, heavy rains and terrifying lightning are seen, while the sky remains as it was and the earth likewise. So this is a sign indicating a free-choosing agent (fa'il mukhtar) who makes one matter continue while the place changes, and removes another matter while the place remains fixed.

The third issue: Just as He placed the sky before the earth, He placed what comes from the sky, namely the lightning and the rain, before what comes from the earth, namely the growing of plants and the giving of life.

The fourth issue: Just as there are benefits in the sending down of rain and the growth of trees, so too there is benefit in the lightning and thunder preceding the rain. This is because when lightning appears, whoever is not under shelter fears being soaked and prepares for it; whoever has a cistern or a reservoir needs water; whoever has crops arranges the channels of water. Also, the Arabs who dwell in the desert would not know the grassy lands unless they had seen the lightning flashing from one side rather than another. Know that the benefits of lightning, even if they are not apparent to those who dwell in towns, are apparent to the nomads. For this reason He made the lightning's preceding the sending down of water from the sky a blessing and a sign. As for its being a sign, it is evident: in the cloud there is nothing but water and air, yet fire comes out of it so that it burns mountains, which is extremely strange. Therefore there must be a creator, and He is God.

The philosophers said: the cloud has density and subtlety in comparison with air and water. Air is subtler than it, and water is denser. When a strong wind blows and tears through the cloud violently, the sound of thunder arises, and fire comes out of it, like a body touching another body violently. This is like the fire that comes out when a stone strikes iron.

If someone says: the stone and the iron are solid bodies, while the cloud and the wind are moist bodies. They reply: but the movement of a human hand is weak, while the movement of the wind is strong, uprooting trees. We say to them: lightning and thunder are two originated things (hadithan) that must have a cause, and it has been established by proof that every originated thing is from God; therefore they are from God. Then we say: suppose the matter is as you say; the blowing of that strong wind is among the wondrous originated events, and it must have a cause that ends at the Necessary Existent (wajib al-wujud). So it is a sign for the intelligent person of God's power, however you suppose it.

The fifth issue: He said here: ﴿for a people who use their reason﴾. Since the birth of a child from its parent is an ordinary, regular matter with little variation, the common delusions could come to think that this is by nature (al-tab'), because the regular is closer to nature than the varied. But lightning and rain are not a regular matter that never fails, since they fall in one land and not another, at one time and not another, sometimes strong and sometimes weak. Therefore it is more evident to reason as an indication of a free-choosing agent. So He said: it is a sign for whoever has reason, if he does not reflect with complete reflection.

* *

Then God Most High said: ﴿And among His signs is that the heaven and the earth stand by His command. Then, when He calls you with a single call from the earth, behold, you will come forth.﴾

When He mentioned some of the accidents of the heaven and the earth, He mentioned some of their necessary attributes, namely their standing. For the earth, because of its heaviness, a person marvels at its standing still and not falling. And the heaven: a person marvels at its height and its stability without pillars. This is among the necessary attributes, for the earth does not leave its place in which it is, and the heaven likewise does not leave its place in which it is. If it is said that they move in their place like a millstone, yet the sane have agreed that they do not leave their place. This is a clear sign, because their being in the place they are in and upon the place they are upon is among the possible matters, while their being in other than that place is also possible. So it would be possible for them to leave it. Since they did not leave, this is a preference of the possible over its alternative, and that cannot occur except by a free-choosing agent.

The philosophers said: the earth's being in the place it is in is natural to it, because it is the heaviest of things, and the heavy seeks the centre, while the light seeks the surrounding sphere. As for the heaven, its being in its place, if it has a place, is by its essence; so its standing in them is by its own nature. We say: it has been said many times before that the doctrine of nature is false. What we add here is that you agreed with us that what is permissible for one of two like things is permissible for the other like thing. But the concave of the sphere does not differ from its convex in nature, so it is permissible for its concave to occur in the place of its convex, and this is by departure and cessation. Thus cessation from a place is possible, especially for the lowest heaven, since by your own school it is bounded by directions too. The earth also could undergo circular motion as you say of the heaven. So its non-existence and its stillness are only by a free-choosing agent.

Issues concerning the verse:

The first issue: God mentioned two matters from each category. From the selves He mentioned: ﴿He created for you﴾, deriving evidence from the creation of the pair. From the horizons He mentioned the heaven and the earth in His saying: ﴿the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾. From the necessary attributes of man: the difference of tongues and colours; from his separable accidents: sleep and seeking. From the accidents of the horizons: lightning and rain; from their necessary attributes: the standing of the heaven and the standing of the earth. This is because one (proof) suffices for an affirmation of the truth, while the second yields conjecture, and another's statement yields its confirmation. For this reason Abraham, peace be upon him, said: ﴿Yes, but that my heart may be at rest﴾ [al-Baqara 2:260].

The second issue: His saying ﴿by His command﴾ means: by His word, "Be" (qawman), or by His will for their standing. This is because, according to the Mu'tazila, command coincides with will, while according to us it is not so. Yet the dispute concerns the command that is for obligation (al-taklif), not the command that is for origination (al-takwin). For we do not dispute with them that His saying "Be" (kun) and "Be, O fire, cool" ﴿Be cool, O fire﴾ [al-Anbiya' 21:69] coincides with the will.

The third issue: He said here ﴿And among His signs is that [it] stands﴾, and before it He said ﴿And among His signs is that He shows you﴾, and He did not say "that He shows you". Although some exegetes said that "an" (that) is implied there, meaning "from His signs (that He shows you)", so that it becomes like a verbal noun with "an". This is because standing, since it does not change, He turned the verb with "an" away from the future tense and made it a verbal noun, since the future tense indicates renewal. As for lightning, since it is among matters that renew at one time and not another, He mentioned it with the future-tense form and did not attach any verbal particles to it.

The fourth issue: He mentioned six proofs, and in four of them He said ﴿Indeed in that are signs﴾. He did not say it for the first, which is His saying ﴿And among His signs is that He created you from dust﴾, nor for the other, which is His saying ﴿And among His signs is that the heaven and the earth stand﴾. As for the first, this is because His saying after it ﴿And among His signs is that He created for you﴾ is also a proof from the selves; the creation of the selves and the creation of the spouses are from one category, as we explained, except that He mentioned two matters from each category for the sake of affirmation through repetition. So when He said ﴿Indeed in that are signs﴾, it refers back to both. As for the standing of the heaven and the earth, we say: regarding the heavenly signs He mentioned that they are signs for those who know, and for a people who use reason, because of their manifestness. Since at the beginning of the matter it is manifest, at the end of the matter, after the enumeration of proofs, it becomes even more manifest. So He did not distinguish anyone from anyone in that, and He mentioned what it signifies, which is His power over the resurrection, and He said: ﴿Then, when He calls you with a single call from the earth, behold, you will come forth.﴾ There are issues concerning this:

The first issue: What is the reason for the conjunction "then" (thumma), and to what does "then" attach? We say its meaning, and God knows best, is: when He has shown you the perfection of His power through these signs, after that He informs you and makes you know that when He says to the decayed bones, "Come forth from the graves," they come forth alive.

The second issue: The speaker's saying "So-and-so called so-and-so from the mountain" may mean that the calling is from the mountain, as the speaker says, "O so-and-so, ascend to the mountain," so it is said, "He called him from the mountain." It may also mean that the one called is called from the mountain, as the speaker says, "O so-and-so, come down from the mountain," so it is said, "He called him from the mountain." It is not hidden from the intelligent that calling does not come from the earth if the caller is God. So the one called is called from the earth, meaning: you are in the earth, and He calls you from it, and you come forth.

The third issue: His saying ﴿behold [idha]﴾: we have explained that it is for sudden occurrence (lil-mufaja'a), meaning that it happens by "Be," and it is.

The fourth issue: He said here ﴿behold, you will come forth﴾, and in the creation of man at first He said: ﴿then, behold, you are humans spreading out﴾ [al-Rum 30:20]. We say: there, there is creation, measuring, gradualness, and delay until the dust becomes receptive to life, and then He breathes into it His spirit, and behold, it is a human being. But in the resurrection there is no gradualness or delay; rather there is a call and a coming forth. Therefore He did not say "then" here.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 30, verses 26–27:

Then the Exalted said: ﴿To Him belongs whoever is in the heavens and the earth; all are devoutly obedient to Him.﴾ ﴿It is He who originates creation, then repeats it, and that is easier for Him.﴾ ﴿To Him belongs the highest description in the heavens and the earth, and He is the Almighty, the All-Wise.﴾

When He mentioned the signs, and their indication was the power to resurrect (al-hashr), which is the second principle, and the oneness (al-wahdaniyyah) of God, which is the first principle, He alluded to them with His words: ﴿To Him belongs whoever is in the heavens and the earth.﴾ That is, He has no partner at all, because everyone in the heavens and everyone on the earth belongs to Him and is under His dominion, so all of them are submissive and obedient to Him. A partner would be a rival and an equal, so He has no partner at all. Then He mentioned the other indication, saying: ﴿It is He who originates creation, then repeats it, and that is easier for Him.﴾ That is, in your estimation, repetition is easier than initiation, because one who does something for the first time finds it difficult, and once he has done the like of it afterward, it becomes easier. It has also been said that the meaning is: "It is easy for Him," as is said in the saying of the speaker "God is greater" (Allahu akbar), meaning "great." It has also been said that the meaning is: "It is easier for Him," that is, repetition is easier for the Creator than initiation, because in the beginning there is a clot (ʿalaqah), then a lump of flesh (mudghah), then flesh, then bone, then he is formed as a human being, then he comes out as a child who grows up, and so on, so all of that is difficult for Him. As for repetition, he comes out as a complete human being by "Be!" (kun), so it is easier for Him. The first view is more correct, and it is upon it that we speak, so we say: "It is easier" may be understood in this way, because in initiation there is the creation of the parts and their composition, and repetition is a composition. There is no doubt that one matter is easier than two matters, and this does not necessitate that the other act involves difficulty. To clarify this, we say: "The easy" (al-hayyin) is that in which the doer does not become weary, and "the easier" (al-ahwan) is that in which the doer does not become weary by a stronger degree. So if someone says that a strong man does not become weary from moving a grain of barley from one place to another, and the listener accepts this, then if he says that He does not become weary from moving a mustard seed, that would be a rational statement that remains upon its literal meaning.
* * *
Then the Exalted said: ﴿To Him belongs the highest description in the heavens and the earth, and He is the Almighty, the All-Wise.﴾ That is, our statement "it is easier for Him" yields two meanings. One of them: that which involves weariness for the other, as one says that moving the light is easier than moving the heavy. The other: the sense of priority we have mentioned, without necessarily implying weariness in the other. So His words ﴿To Him belongs the highest description﴾ indicate that His being easier in the second sense does not imply the first. Here there is a point mentioned by the author of al-Kashshaf, namely that God the Exalted said elsewhere: ﴿It is easy for Me﴾ [Maryam: 9], and here He said: "and it is easier for Him," placing the word "for Me" first there and delaying it here. This is because the meaning mentioned there, that it is easy, is the creation of a child from an old woman, which is difficult for others and is not easy except for Him, so He said: ﴿It is easy for Me﴾ [Maryam: 9], meaning "not for anyone other than Me." As for here, the meaning described as easier is repetition, and repetition is easier for every originator, so He said: "and it is easier for Him," not in the sense of restriction (al-hasr). Thus the fronting there was for restriction. His words ﴿To Him belongs the highest description in the heavens and the earth﴾ have meaning according to the first aspect, which is our statement "easier for Him in relation to you," and they have meaning according to the aspect we mentioned. As for the first aspect, when He said ﴿To Him belongs the highest description﴾, and this was a parable struck for the people on earth, it conveys that He has the highest description among the examples of people, who are the inhabitants of the earth, and does not convey that He has the highest description among the examples of the angels. So He said: ﴿To Him belongs the highest description in the heavens and the earth﴾, meaning: this is a parable struck for you, and ﴿To Him belongs the highest description﴾ from this parable and from every parable struck in the heavens. As for the second aspect, its meaning is that He has the highest description, that is, His act, even though He is likened to your act and described by it; yet His essence is not like anything, so He has the highest description. This is related from Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with him and his father. It has also been said: "the highest description" means the supreme attribute, which is "there is no god but God." His words ﴿He is the Almighty, the All-Wise﴾ mean: perfect in power over possible things, encompassing in knowledge of all existing things, so He knows the parts in their places and is able to gather them and compose them.

Commentary of al-Razi (*Mafatih al-Ghayb*) on surah 30, verse 28:

Then the Exalted said: ﴿He has set forth for you an example from yourselves: Do you have, among those whom your right hands possess, partners in what We have provided for you, so that you are equal in it and you fear them as you fear one another among yourselves? Thus do We detail the signs for a people who reason.﴾

When He had shown the return (of creation) and His power over it through the example, after the two proofs, He also showed the Oneness (of God) through the example, after the proof. Its meaning is that a man may have a slave who is not his partner in his property, and who does not have a dignity equal to that of his master. How, then, could the servants of God be partners with Him? And how could they have a greatness like the greatness of God, the Exalted, so that they might be worshipped? In the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: There should be some resemblance between the example and that which is exemplified. If there is a difference between them, it may either confirm the meaning of the example or weaken it. Here the aspect of resemblance is known. As for the difference, it also exists and it is emphatic, and this is in several respects.

The first: His words ﴿from yourselves﴾, meaning: He has set forth for you an example from yourselves, despite their insignificance, deficiency and weakness, and He has compared Himself to you, despite His greatness, perfection and power.

The second: His words ﴿from among what your right hands possess﴾, meaning: your slave has, over him, the ownership of the hand (*milk al-yad*), which is transient (*ṭāri'*), capable of transfer and of ending. Transfer happens through sale and other means, and ending happens through manumission. But the one owned by God has no exit from God's ownership in any way whatsoever. So if it is not permissible for the slave of your right hands to be a partner to you, even though he may become like you in every respect, indeed he is already like you in humanity, so that you have no right to dispose of his spirit and his humanity by killing or cutting, and you have no right to prevent him from worship and from fulfilling his needs, then how can it be permissible for the one owned by God, who is owned by Him in every respect, to be His partner?

The third: His words ﴿among partners in what We have provided for you﴾, meaning: what you possess is in reality not yours, but comes from God and from His provision, and what comes from God is in reality His. So if it is not permissible for there to be a partner with you in your property in terms of its name, how then can it be permissible for Him to have a partner in what belongs to Him in reality? His words ﴿so that you are equal in it﴾ mean: are you and your slaves equal in any of what you own? No, they are not. Therefore God has no partner in anything He owns. Rather, everything belongs to God. So those whose divinity you claim own nothing at all, not even the weight of a speck of dust in a mustard seed. Therefore they are not worshipped for their greatness, nor for a benefit that might reach you from them. As for your saying, "These are our intercessors," this is not so, because is a slave, in your view, possessed of a dignity like that of free men? When a slave, despite his equality with you in reality and in attribute, has no dignity in your eyes, how then can it be with the slaves who have no equality whatsoever with the owner in any respect? It is to this that He alludes in His words ﴿you fear them as you fear yourselves﴾.

The second issue: By this He negated all the aspects of the goodness of worship from others, because if others are not fit for partnership, they have neither ownership nor sovereignty. Therefore they have no greatness for which they might be worshipped, nor is any benefit expected from them, since they do not own anything, so that they might be worshipped for benefit. Nor do they have strength or power, because they are servants, and a servant who is owned has power over nothing. So do not fear them as you fear yourselves. How, then, would you fear them more than you fear one another, to the point of worshipping them out of fear?

* * *

Then the Exalted said: ﴿Thus do We detail the signs for a people who reason.﴾ That is: We clarify them through proofs and decisive demonstrations, through examples and persuasive illustrations, for a people who reason. That is, after this, the matter is not hidden except from one who has no intellect.

Then God Most High said: ﴿Rather, those who wronged followed their own desires without knowledge. So who can guide one whom God has led astray? They have no helpers.﴾ That is, it is not permissible for the owned to be associated with the Owner, but those who associated partners followed their desires without knowledge, and affirmed partners without any proof. Then He made clear that this happens by the will of God, through His saying: ﴿So who can guide one whom God has led astray?﴾ That is, these are the ones God has led astray, so there is no guide for them. Therefore their speech should not grieve you. And there is a subtle point here: His saying ﴿So who can guide one whom God has led astray?﴾ reinforces what came before. For when He said, "Because God has no partner in any way," and then said, "Rather, the polytheists associate partners [with Him] without knowledge," it could be said: You have attributed to them an action contrary to His pleasure, whereas the Mighty Lord is one whose servant cannot act in a way that opposes His pleasure. So He said: That is not by their own independence, but by the will of God. ﴿And they have no helpers﴾: when they abandoned God, God abandoned them, and those they took [as helpers] do not avail them anything, so they have no helper.
* * *
Then God Most High said: ﴿So set your face toward the religion, as a upright monotheist, the natural disposition [fitrah] of God upon which He created mankind. There is no altering of the creation of God.﴾ That is, when the matter has become clear and the oneness [of God] has become manifest, and the polytheist has not been guided, then do not turn your attention to them, and set your face toward the religion. His saying ﴿So set your face toward the religion﴾ means: turn wholly toward the religion. He expressed the Essence by "face," as He said: ﴿Everything will perish except His face﴾ [al-Qasas: 88], that is, His Essence with its attributes. His saying ﴿ḥanīfan﴾ means inclining away from everything other than it: turn toward the religion and incline away from everything, that is, let there be nothing else in your heart so that you would return to it. This is close in meaning to His saying: ﴿And do not be among the polytheists.﴾ Then God Most High said: ﴿The natural disposition of God﴾, that is, adhere to the natural disposition of God, which is monotheism, for God created people upon it when He took them from the loins of Adam and asked them: ﴿Am I not your Lord?﴾ [al-A'raf: 172], and they said: "Yes." His saying Most High ﴿There is no altering of the creation of God﴾ has several interpretations. Some exegetes said: this is consolation for the Prophet ﷺ regarding grief over his people not believing, so He said: they were created for wretchedness, and whoever is written as wretched will not be made happy. It was also said: ﴿There is no altering of the creation of God﴾ means that monotheism is firmly rooted in them, with no change to it, so that even if you asked them who created the heavens and the earth, they would say: God. However, innate faith (al-iman al-fitri) is not sufficient. It may also be said that God created creation for His worship, and they are all His servants; ﴿There is no altering of the creation of God﴾ means that their being servants is not like a slave's being a servant to a human, who may pass from him to another and leave his ownership through manumission. Rather, there is no departure of creation from worship and servitude. This serves to refute the view of those who say: worship is for attaining perfection, and the servant becomes perfect through worship so that no obligation remains upon him; and the view of the polytheists: that the deficient is not fit to worship God, and that man only worshiped the stars, and the stars are God's servants; and the view of the Christians that Jesus was one in whom God incarnated and so became a god. He said: ﴿There is no altering of the creation of God﴾, rather all of them are servants, and there is no escape for them from that.
* * *
Then God Most High said: ﴿That is the upright religion﴾, which has no crookedness in it, ﴿but most people do not know﴾ that this is the straight religion.

Then He, exalted, said: ﴿Turning penitently to Him, and fear Him, and establish the prayer, and do not be among the polytheists﴾ ﴿Of those who divided their religion and became sects, each faction rejoicing in what it has﴾.

When He said "ḥanīfan" (inclining away from everything else), He said: ﴿turning penitently to Him﴾, meaning turning toward Him with devotion. The address in His words ﴿So set your face﴾ is to the Prophet, but what is meant is all the believers. His words ﴿and fear Him﴾ mean: when you turn toward Him and abandon this world, do not feel secure so that you neglect His worship; rather, fear Him, persist in worship, and establish the prayer, that is, be worshippers at the time of attaining nearness just as you were before that. Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 30, verse 33:

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And when harm touches mankind, they call upon their Lord, turning back to Him in repentance. Then when He gives them a taste of mercy from Himself, behold, a party of them associates others with their Lord.﴾

When He had explained Tawhid (Oneness of God) through proof and through example, He explained that they have a state by which they are recognized, although at some times they deny it, and this is the state of hardship. For when their hope is cut off from everything, they return to God and find themselves in need of something unlike these things, seeking deliverance from it: ﴿Then when He gives them a taste of mercy from Himself, behold, a party of them associates others with their Lord.﴾ That is, when We deliver them, they associate others with their Lord, and say, "I was delivered by the connection of such-and-such star with so-and-so, and by such-and-such idol." No; rather, one should not believe that he was delivered by the means of so-and-so, for if this is apparent, it is a hidden shirk. An example of this: a man in the sea is overtaken by drowning, so God prepares for him a plank, which a wind drives toward him, and he clings to it and is saved, and he says, "I was delivered by a plank," or a man on whom a beast of prey came, so God sends to him a man who helps him, and he says, "Zayd rescued me." If this is based on belief, then it is hidden shirk; and if it means that God delivered me at the hand of Zayd, it is more hidden. And in this there are several issues:

The first issue: His saying, ﴿gives them a taste﴾ (adhaqahum) contains a subtle point. This is because the word dhawq (tasting) is used for a small amount; for by custom, one who eats a large quantity does not say "I tasted." It is also used in negation, as in "I did not taste food in his house," negating the small amount so that the negation of the large amount follows a fortiori. Then, since that mercy was temporary and cut off, and was not lasting in the Hereafter—for they will have punishment in the Hereafter—He said "gives them a taste."

For this reason He said regarding the punishment: ﴿Taste the touch of Saqar﴾ [al-Qamar: 48], ﴿Taste what you used to do﴾ [al-Ankabut: 55], ﴿Taste! Indeed you are the mighty, the noble﴾ [al-Dukhan: 49]; because God's punishment reaching the servant, compared with the mercy reaching other servants, is extremely little.

The second issue: His saying, ﴿from Himself﴾ (minhu), that is, from the harm. In this specification lies the benefit we mentioned, namely that the mercy is not absolute for them; it is only from that particular harm alone, and as for the deferred harm, they do not taste mercy from it.

The third issue: Here He said ﴿behold, a party of them﴾ (fariq minhum), and in al-Ankabut He said: ﴿Then when He delivered them to the land, behold, they associate others﴾ [al-Ankabut: 65], and did not say "a party." This is because what is mentioned there is a specific harm, which is the terror of the sea, and those delivered from it, relative to creation, are few; and those among them who do not associate others after deliverance are a party of extreme fewness. So He did not make the polytheists a "party," because of the fewness of those who came out of the polytheists. As for what is mentioned here, harm in general, it encompasses the harm of land and sea, sicknesses and terrors, and those delivered from kinds of harm are a great multitude; indeed all people have fallen into some harm and been delivered from it. And those who, after deliverance, do not remain polytheists in respect of all kinds, when gathered, are a great number, and they are all the Muslims, for they have been delivered from harm and did not remain polytheists. As for the Muslims, not all of them were delivered from the harm of the sea; so since those delivered from harm among the believers are a great multitude, He made the remainder a "party."

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 30, verses 34–35:

Then He said, exalted is He: ﴿So that they may deny what We have given them. Enjoy yourselves, for you will soon know.﴾ ﴿Or have We sent down to them an authority which speaks of what they have been associating with Him?﴾

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So that they may deny what We have given them. Enjoy yourselves, for you will soon know.﴾ Its tafsir has already been mentioned in Surat al-Ankabut. What remains is an explanation of the benefit of the address here in His words ﴿fa-tamatta'u﴾ (enjoy yourselves), and of its absence there in His words ﴿wa-liyatamatta'u fa-sawfa ya'lamun﴾ (and let them enjoy themselves, for they will soon know). We say: since the harm mentioned there was a single harm, it was possible that among those being addressed in that place there was no one delivered from that harm, so they were not addressed directly. But since what is mentioned here is harm in general, and no group of people is free from harm, the one present may be validly addressed as being among them, so He addressed them directly.

* * *

Then He said, exalted is He: ﴿Or have We sent down to them an authority which speaks of what they have been associating with Him?﴾ Since His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Rather, those who wronged followed their desires﴾ [al-Rum: 29] preceded, meaning: the polytheists say what they have no knowledge of, rather they know otherwise, for at the time of harm they turn back to Allah. This is confirmed by the interrogative used in the sense of denial, i.e., We did not send down any authority for what they say. In this there are several issues:

The first issue: ﴿am﴾ (or) is interrogative and does not occur except in the middle of a sentence, as one of them said:

O gazelle of al-Wa'sa, between Julajil and the sand dunes, are you (the one), or is it Umm Salim?

What is the interrogative before it? We say: its implied meaning is: when these proofs became manifest against their obstinacy, then what shall we say? Do they follow desires without knowledge? Or do they have evidence for what they say? The second is not the case, so the first is determined.

The second issue: His saying ﴿fa-huwa yatakallamu﴾ (so it speaks) is a metaphor, as one says "his book speaks of such and such." In it there is a subtle meaning: the one who speaks without evidence is as if he has no speech, because speech is that which is heard, and what is not accepted is as if it was not heard. Thus the speaker is as if he did not speak it. And what has no evidence is not accepted. So if denying speech to the speaker when there is no evidence is valid and fitting, then affirming speech for the evidence is also valid and fitting.

When He explained the state of the manifest polytheist (mushrik), whose polytheism is evident, He then explained the state of the one below him, whose worship of God is for the sake of this world. The first is like one who serves under compulsion out of fear of punishment, and the second is like one who serves as a hired worker in expectation of wages. Neither of them is among those enrolled in the register of those who are paid and listed in the ledgers, who receive their provision whether or not there is work to be done. Likewise, these two types are not among the believers who have a provision with their Lord.

There is also an issue here: His saying, ﴿they rejoice in it﴾, indicates the lowness of their aspiration and the shortness of their vision, for their joy is in what has reached them, not in what it comes from. ﴿So give the near of kin his due, and the needy, and the wayfarer. That is better for those who seek the Face of God, and it is they who are the successful.﴾

The connection of this verse with what precedes it is that God, having explained that worship should not be confined to a state of hardship, as in His words ﴿And when harm touches people, they call upon their Lord﴾ [Ar-Rum: 33], nor confined to a state of obtaining something of this world, as is the habit of the one who is al-mudawkar al-mutasalsis (a person of ill character), who worships God when he is in the khawaniq (Sufi lodges) and ribats (hospices) for a loaf of bread and a dish of butter, and when he is alone with himself does not remember God, said: ﴿And when We let people taste mercy, they rejoice in it.﴾ He then explained that a person should be in a state of having provision expanded or restricted and should look to God, the Creator and Provider, so that guidance toward exalting God is attained. Faith has two parts: exalting the command of God, and compassion toward the creation of God. So after that He said, ﴿So give the near of kin his due, and the needy, and the wayfarer.﴾ There is another connection as well: God, having explained that God expands provision and restricts it, a person should not hold back from doing good, for when God expands provision it does not diminish by spending, and when He restricts it, it does not increase by withholding. Concerning this verse there are several issues:

The first issue: concerning the specification of these three categories by mention, apart from others, although God mentioned the eight categories in the matter of alms. We say: here He intended to specify who must be treated with kindness by everyone who has wealth, whether it is subject to zakat or not, and whether it has passed its full year or not, because the aim here is general compassion. These three must be treated with kindness even if the giver has no surplus wealth. As for the near relative, his maintenance is obligatory even if no zakat is due on the wealth, such as property or wealth on which a year has not passed.

The needy (miskin) is similar, for he is one who has nothing; if he remains in the grip of need until he reaches extreme hardship, it is obligatory for one who has the means to relieve his need, even if no zakat is due on that person. Likewise, one who is stranded in a desert with only a last animal by which he can be brought to safety is obligated to do so, even if no zakat is due on him. The faqir (poor person) is included within the miskin, because if someone bequeaths something to the needy, it is also spent on the poor. When you consider the remaining categories, you see that wealth is not obligatorily spent on them except on those upon whom zakat is due; this is taken into account regarding the amil (zakat collector), the mukatab (slave seeking manumission), the muallafa (those whose hearts are to be reconciled), and the debtor. Next, know that according to the school of Abu Hanifa, may God have mercy on him, who said: "The miskin is one who has something," we say: even if that is the case, there is no dispute that applying the term miskin to one who has nothing is permissible, so the application here is in that sense, and the faqir enters into it all the more.

The second issue: concerning the precedence of some over others. We say: since relieving the need of the near relative is obligatory, whether he is in hardship and extreme hunger or not, he takes precedence over one whose need does not obligate relief from non-zakat wealth unless he is in hardship. And since the need of the miskin is not specific to one place, he takes precedence over one whose need is specific to a particular place rather than another.

The third issue: He mentioned the near relatives in all places with this wording, namely dhu al-qurba (those of near kin), and did not mention the miskin with the wording dhu al-maskana (one possessing poverty). This is because kinship does not renew; it is a fixed thing, and dhu (possessor of) with such a noun is said only of what is established. For whoever has a sound opinion once, or obtains standing for a single day, or is found to have excellence at a time, is called dhu ra'y (one of sound opinion), dhu jah (one of standing), and dhu fadl (one of excellence). But when that becomes lasting for him, or it is found in him frequently, he is called dhu al-ra'y and dhu al-fadl. So His words ﴿dha al-qurba﴾ indicate that this is a firm and established right. As for poverty (maskana), it comes and goes; for this reason He said: ﴿a needy person in misery﴾ [Al-Balad: 16]. The miskin remains in the state of being in misery as long as his poverty lasts, or it is so in most cases.

The fourth issue: He said, ﴿So give the near of kin his due﴾, then He conjoined the needy and the wayfarer and did not say, "So give the near of kin and the needy and the wayfarer their due." This is because the second wording, where the speech first begins and the conjunction comes into it, and the first wording, where the conjunction is applied to the speech, differ. It is as if He is saying: "Give the near of kin his due," then He mentions the needy and the wayfarer as following. For this reason, when a king says, "Let so-and-so enter, and so-and-so too," it carries more honor than if he says, "Let so-and-so and so-and-so enter." To this the Prophet (ﷺ) pointed in his saying: "Evil is the orator of the people, you," when a man said: "Whoever obeys God and His Messenger is rightly guided, and whoever disobeys them both has gone astray," and did not say, "and whoever disobeys God and His Messenger."

* * *

The fifth issue: His words ﴿that is better﴾ may mean "that is better than other things," or it may be said "that is good in itself," even if it is not compared to something else, as in His words: ﴿And do good﴾ [Al-Hajj: 77] and ﴿So race to good deeds﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 148]. The second is preferable, because it does not need an implied element, and because it is more beneficial, since good compared to something else may be of a lower rank; when a rank is lowered, it is compared to something else, as one says: "Silence is better than lying." What is good in itself is what is beneficial and righteous action that elevates.

The sixth issue: His words ﴿for those who seek the Face of God﴾ point to the fact that what matters is the intention, not the act itself. Whoever spends all his wealth to be seen by people does not attain the rank of one who gives a loaf of bread for God. His words ﴿the Face of God﴾ mean that his giving is for God alone; whoever gives for Paradise has not intended the Face of God, but has intended a creation of God.

The seventh issue: How did He say ﴿and it is they who are the successful﴾ when success has other conditions, which are those mentioned in His words: ﴿The believers have certainly succeeded﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 1]? We say: every attribute mentioned there confers success, so His words ﴿and those who are payers of zakat﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 4] and His words ﴿and those who are faithful to their trusts and their covenants﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 8], and so on, are conjoined to the successful: meaning, this one is successful, and that one is successful, and that other one is successful. It may not be said that success is not attained by one who gives charity but does not pray. We say: this is like the saying of one who says: "The scholar is honored," meaning in view of his knowledge. Then if he is flogged for fornication as a deterrent, or his hand is cut off for theft, that saying is not invalidated, unless one says: "That is only because he committed immorality." Likewise, giving wealth for the sake of God confers success, except where there is an impediment from committing a forbidden act or abandoning an obligatory one.

The eighth issue: Why did He not mention other acts, such as prayer and others? We say: prayer has been mentioned earlier, because the address here with His words ﴿So give﴾ is to the Prophet (ﷺ), and others follow him. He had said to him earlier ﴿So set your face toward the religion, inclining to truth﴾ and said:

﴿Turning back to Him, and fear Him, and establish prayer﴾ [Ar-Rum: 31].

The ninth issue: His words ﴿and it is they who are the successful﴾ imply restriction, and He had said at the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah: ﴿And it is they who are the successful﴾, referring to those who establish prayer, give zakat, believe in what was sent down to His Messenger and what was sent down before him, and in the Hereafter. If the successful were restricted to those mentioned in Surat al-Baqarah, then this person would be outside of them, so how could he be successful? We say: this is that, because we have shown that His words ﴿So set your face toward the religion﴾ are connected with this discourse. So when he performs prayer, gives wealth, and intends the Face of God, it is established that he is a believer, who establishes prayer, pays zakat, and acknowledges the Hereafter, and so he becomes like those mentioned in al-Baqarah.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And whatever you give in usury so that it may increase within the property of people will not increase with Allah. But whatever you give in zakah, seeking the countenance of Allah — those are the ones who will receive multiplied reward.﴾

He mentioned this as an incitement, meaning: if one of you is asked to repay one with two, you are eager for it and give it, but that does not increase with Allah, whereas zakah grows with Allah, as the Prophet (ﷺ) informed: "Indeed, charity falls into the hand of the All-Merciful, and it grows until it becomes like a mountain." So your readiness to give zakah should be greater. As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And whatever you give in zakah, seeking the countenance of Allah — those are the ones who will receive multiplied reward﴾, meaning: those are the people of multiplied reward, like the wealthy man's gift to one of means, and the least of that is tenfold. Each is a parable for what is given, in that it is a good deed, not in the amount. So it should not be understood that whoever gives a loaf of bread, Allah gives him ten loaves. Rather, its meaning is that the reward which his act deserves on the basis of mercy, Allah multiplies ten times on the basis of bounty. Thus for a single loaf there is a palace in Paradise containing everything, as a reward considered in terms of mercy, and ten palaces like it considered in terms of bounty.

Its example in the visible world: a great king accepted a gift from his servant whose value is one dirham. If he compensated him with ten dirhams, that would not be generosity; rather, if it is his custom to give a thousand for the like of that, then when he gives him ten thousand, he has multiplied the reward for him.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 30, verse 40:

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿It is Allah who created you, then provided for you, then will cause you to die, then will bring you to life. Is there any of your partners who does anything of that? Glory be to Him, and high is He above what they associate with Him.﴾

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿It is Allah who created you﴾ means He brought you into existence. ﴿Then provided for you﴾ means He kept you in existence, for accidents (ʿaraḍ) are created and are not self-subsisting. ﴿Then will cause you to die, then will bring you to life. Is there any of your partners who does anything of that?﴾ In this verse He combined the affirmation of the two foundations: the Resurrection (ḥashr) and the Oneness of God (tawḥīd). As for the Resurrection, it is by His saying ﴿then will bring you to life﴾, and the proof is His power over creation from the beginning. As for the Oneness, it is by His saying ﴿Is there any of your partners who does anything of that?﴾ Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Glory be to Him, and high is He above what they associate with Him.﴾ As for His saying "Glory be to Him" (subḥānahu), it means: glorify Him with glorification, that is, declare Him far above, and do not describe Him with association. As for His saying ﴿and high is He (wa-taʿālā)﴾, it means that such a thing is not permissible for Him. This is because one who is not characterized by something may still be susceptible to it; so when He says "glorify Him" it means do not describe Him with association, and when He says "and high is He" it is as if He said: such a thing is not permissible for Him.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 30, verse 41:

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Corruption has appeared on land and sea because of what the hands of people have earned, so that He may let them taste part of what they have done, that they may return.﴾

The connection of this verse with what precedes it is that polytheism (shirk) is the cause of corruption, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Had there been in them gods other than Allah, they would have been ruined﴾ [al-Anbiya: 22]. Since polytheism is the cause, Allah made their display of polytheism the means by which corruption appears. Had He dealt with them according to what their saying requires, ﴿the heavens and the earth would have been corrupted﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 71], as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿The heavens are almost rent asunder from it, and the earth splits open, and the mountains collapse in ruin﴾ [Maryam: 90]. To this He alluded with His words: ﴿so that He may let them taste part of what they have done.﴾

Scholars differed concerning His words: ﴿on land and sea.﴾ Some exegetes said: the intended meaning is the fear of the flood on land and sea. Others said: the non-growth of some lands and the salinity of the waters of the seas. Still others said: the intended meaning of "sea" is cities, for the Arabs call cities "seas" because the foundations of their construction are upon water. It may also be said that the appearance of corruption in the sea is the scarcity of the waters of springs, for they are among the seas.

Know that every corruption is caused by polytheism, but polytheism may exist in action without speech and belief, and it is then called immorality (fisq) and disobedience ('isyan). This is because sin is an act that does not belong to Allah but to the self; so the one who commits immorality is a polytheist through his deed. The utmost that can be said is that polytheism in action does not necessitate eternal abiding (in Hellfire), because the root of a person is his heart and his tongue. When nothing of these two proceeds except monotheism, the bodily polytheism is removed by means of them.

His words: ﴿so that He may let them taste part of what they have done﴾ — we have mentioned that this is not the full recompense for them nor the whole of what their fabrication requires. His words: ﴿that they may return﴾ mean, as one who expects their return does; although Allah knows that whomever He misguides will not return. Yet people suppose that if some such thing were done to them, return would occur from them. This is like a master who knows that his slave will not be deterred by words: someone says, "Why do you not discipline him with words?" When it is said, "It does not benefit," it may occur to him that there is still hope of some benefit. Then when he rebukes him and he is not deterred, the truth of the master's words becomes manifest to him and his heart is reassured.

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Say: Travel through the earth and see what was the end of those before, most of whom were polytheists.﴾

When He had shown their condition, namely the emergence of corruption in their affairs because of the corruption of their statements, He showed them the destruction of their likes and counterparts, those whose deeds were like their deeds. So He said: ﴿Say: Travel through the earth and see what was the end of those before﴾, that is, the people of Noah, ʿĀd and Thamūd. This is an arrangement of the utmost beauty. For at the time of bestowal and kindness He said: ﴿Allah is He who created you, then provided for you﴾, that is, He gave you existence and then continuance. And at the time of abandonment through transgression He said: ﴿Corruption has appeared on land and sea﴾, that is, He reduced your provision. Then He said, exalted is He: ﴿Travel through the earth﴾, that is, He will annihilate you as He annihilated those before you. It is as if He said: He gave you existence and continuance, and He will take from you existence and continuance. As for the removal of continuance, it is by the appearance of corruption; as for the removal of existence, it is by destruction. In giving, He placed existence before continuance, because existence comes first and then continuance; and in taking away, He placed continuance first, which is persistence, and then existence.

His saying: ﴿most of whom were polytheists﴾ admits three aspects:

The first: that destruction, for the most part, was caused by overt polytheism, although it was also caused by other things, such as destruction through wickedness and disobedience, as happened to the people of the Sabbath.

The second: that every disbeliever who was destroyed was not a polytheist; rather, among them were those who were atheists, denying [the Creator], but they were few, and most disbelievers are polytheists.

The third: that the hasty punishment, when it came, did not single out only the polytheists, as Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And beware of a trial which will not strike exclusively those of you who have done wrong﴾ [al-Anfal: 25]. Rather it fell upon the young children and the insane, but most of them were polytheists.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 30, verses 43–44:

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿So set your face toward the upright religion before there comes a Day which no one can avert from Allah. That Day they will be divided.﴾ ﴿Whoever disbelieves, his disbelief will be upon him, and whoever does righteousness – for themselves they are preparing [a resting place].﴾

When He forbade the disbeliever from what he was upon, He commanded the believer with what he was upon, and He addressed the Prophet (ﷺ) so that the believer would know the excellence of what he is charged with, for He commanded with it the most noble of the prophets. The believers share in the obligation the station of the prophets, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed Allah commanded His believing servants with what He commanded His messenger servants." We have already mentioned its meaning. His saying ﴿before there comes a Day which no one can avert from Allah﴾ may bear two interpretations:

The first: that ﴿from Allah﴾ is connected to His saying ﴿comes﴾.

The second: that what is meant by ﴿which no one can avert from Allah﴾ is that Allah does not turn it back and others are incapable of turning it back, so it must occur. ﴿That Day they will be divided﴾, i.e., they will separate. Then He indicated the separation by His saying: ﴿Whoever disbelieves, his disbelief will be upon him, and whoever does righteousness – for themselves they are preparing [a resting place].﴾ There are several issues in the verse:

The first issue: He said ﴿Whoever disbelieves, his disbelief will be upon him, and whoever does righteousness﴾ and did not say "whoever believes." This is because righteous deeds complete faith, so He mentioned them to urge the one who is obligated toward them. As for disbelief, when it comes, no weight remains for deeds alongside it. Another aspect: disbelief has two kinds:

One: an act, which is associating partners with Allah and affirming it.

The second: an omission, which is failing to reflect and to have faith. So the sane adult who is in the city of the Messenger and does not bring faith is a disbeliever, whether he affirms association or does not. However, faith must be accompanied by righteous deeds, for correct belief is an action of the heart, and the saying "There is no god but Allah" is an action of the tongue, and some of it is necessary.

The second issue: He said ﴿his disbelief will be upon him﴾, using the singular pronoun, and He said ﴿for themselves﴾, using the plural, indicating that mercy is more general than wrath, so it encompasses him, his family and his offspring. As for wrath, it is preceded by mercy and is incumbent upon the one who does evil.

The third issue: He said ﴿his disbelief will be upon him﴾ without specifying, and regarding the believer He said ﴿for themselves they are preparing [a resting place]﴾, affirming the completeness of mercy. For when speaking of good He specified and elaborated as good news, and regarding the other He alluded to it briefly.

Then He said, exalted is He: ﴿That He may reward those who believe and do righteous deeds out of His bounty. Indeed, He does not love the disbelievers.﴾

He mentioned a further detail about what the believer prepares for his good deed and righteous action, namely the recompense that Allah gives him. A king, if he is great and generous, when he promises one of his servants, "I will reward you," the reward reaches him in greater measure than he expects. Then Allah confirmed this with His words, ﴿out of His bounty﴾, meaning: I am the one who rewards, so consider how the reward will be. Moreover, I do not reward you by strict justice, but by bounty, so that hope increases. Then Allah said, ﴿Indeed, He does not love the disbelievers﴾. He threatened them with a warning and did not spell it out, for the reason we have explained. Although, according to the verifier (al-muhaqqiq, a scholar who examines matters rigorously), this general statement is like a detailed one, since the absence of Allah's love is the utmost of punishment. Understand this from one who has a beloved: when he is told that the beloved has promised you dirhams and dinars, how joyful he becomes; and when it is said to him that the beloved said, "I love so-and-so," how great is his delight.

There is also a subtle point here. When Allah attributed disbelief and belief to the servant, He placed the disbeliever first, saying, ﴿Whoever disbelieves, upon him is his disbelief﴾. When He attributed the reward to Himself, He placed the believer first, saying, ﴿That He may reward those who believe﴾. Then He said, ﴿Indeed, He does not love the disbelievers﴾. This is because His words ﴿Whoever disbelieves﴾ are in reality to restrain the disbeliever from disbelief by warning and to forbid him from doing it by threat. His words ﴿and whoever does righteousness﴾ are to encourage the believer. So the prohibition is like a warning and an exhortation for confirmation, and warning comes first with the wise and merciful. As for when He mentioned the reward, He began with goodness, to show generosity and mercy.

If someone says: this would be valid only if the mention were like this in every passage, but it is not so, for in many places Allah has placed the believer's faith before the disbeliever's disbelief, and placed punishment before reward. We say: if Allah enables us to explain this, we will clarify what required its placement first. We say that every word that occurs in the Qur'an has a meaning, and every order that exists has a wisdom, and what is mentioned contrary to this does not reach the level of what the Qur'an has revealed. Let us clarify from among these an example, which is His words, exalted is He: ﴿On that Day they will be separated﴾ [al-Rum: 14], ﴿As for those who believed and did righteous deeds, they will be in a garden, delighted﴾ [al-Rum: 15]. He placed the believer before the disbeliever. Here He mentioned the same meaning in His words, ﴿On that Day they will be divided﴾, meaning they will be separated, and He placed the disbeliever before the believer. We say that there too He placed the disbeliever first in mention, because He had said earlier, ﴿And on the Day the Hour is established, the criminals will be dismayed﴾ [al-Rum: 12]. He mentioned the disbeliever and his dismay, then He said, exalted is He, ﴿And on the Day the Hour is established, on that Day they will be separated﴾. So mentioning the believer alone was necessary, so that the manner of the separation would be made clear by the whole statement, ﴿the criminals will be dismayed﴾, together with His words about the believer, ﴿in a garden they will be made joyful﴾ [al-Rum: 15]. However, Allah, exalted is He, repeated the mention of the criminals a second time for detail, saying, ﴿As for those who disbelieved﴾.

صفحة ١١٥

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And among His signs is that He sends the winds as bearers of good news, and that He lets you taste of His mercy, and that the ships run by His command, and that you may seek of His bounty, and perhaps you will give thanks.﴾

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And among His signs is that He sends the winds as bearers of good news﴾. When He mentioned that the appearance of corruption and destruction is caused by shirk (associating partners with God), He mentioned the appearance of goodness but did not say that it was caused by righteous deeds. This is because, as we have mentioned more than once, the Generous does not mention a return for His beneficence, and He mentions a cause for His harms, lest injustice be imagined in Him. So He said: ﴿He sends the winds as bearers of good news﴾. It was said that this means bearers of rain, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿as good news before His mercy﴾ [al-A'raf: 57], that is, before the rain. It is also possible to say that they are bearers of good news of the improvement of the air and the conditions, for if the winds did not blow, plague and corruption would appear.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿and that He lets you taste of His mercy﴾. This is a conjunction with what we have mentioned, meaning: so that He gives you good news of the goodness of the air and the health of the bodies. ﴿and that He lets you taste of His mercy﴾ by means of the rain. We have mentioned that the verb "adhaqa" (to let taste) is used for a small amount, and since the affairs of this world are small and its comfort is meagre, He said: ﴿that He lets you taste﴾. As for the Hereafter, He will provide for them, widen (His provision) upon them, and make it lasting for them.

﴿and that the ships run by His command, and that you may seek of His bounty, and perhaps you will give thanks﴾. When He attributed the action to the ships, He followed it with His saying: ﴿by His command﴾, that is, the action is apparent upon them, but it is by the command of God. For this reason, when He said: ﴿and that you may seek﴾, attributing it to the servants, He mentioned after it: ﴿of His bounty﴾, that is, nothing is independent of anything else.

In the verse there are several issues.

The first issue concerns the order. We say: there are benefits in the winds. Among them is the improvement of the air, among them is the stirring up of clouds, and among them is the running of ships by them. So He said: ﴿bearers of good news﴾ by the improvement of the air, for the improvement of the air comes into existence from the very blowing, then the rains come after it, then the running of the ships, for it depends upon a test by the human being in repairing the ships and launching them upon the sea, then the seeking of bounty by riding them.

The second issue: He said concerning the verse ﴿corruption has appeared . . . that He may let them taste some of what they have done﴾ [al-Rum: 41], and here He said ﴿and that He lets you taste of His mercy﴾. So He addressed here (with the second person) out of honour, and because His mercy is near to the good-doers; the good-doer is near and so is addressed, while the evildoer is far, so He did not address them. Also, there He said ﴿some of what they have done﴾, and here He said ﴿of His mercy﴾. Thus He attributed what afflicted them to themselves, and He attributed what reached the believer to His mercy. In this there are two meanings:

The first is what we have mentioned: that the Generous does not mention a return for His beneficence and mercy. If it exists, He does not say, "I gave you because you did such and such," but rather says, "This is for you from Me." As for the good deed you have done, its recompense is with Me afterwards.

The second is that what occurs through the act of the servant is small. If He had said, "I sent the winds because of your deed," it would not be a great good news. But when He says, ﴿of His mercy﴾, it is the utmost of good news. There is a third meaning, which is that if He had said, "because of what you have done," that would imply a diminution of their reward in the Hereafter. As for the disbelievers, if He says "because of what you have done," it indicates a lessening of their punishment, and the matter is indeed so.

The third issue: there He said ﴿perhaps they will return﴾ [al-Rum: 41], and here He said: ﴿and perhaps you will give thanks﴾. They said: this is an indication that their being granted gratitude is among the blessings, so He joined it to the blessings.

The fourth issue: He placed this verse last only because among the signs already mentioned, we said that He mentioned two from each category. So He mentioned among the warnings: ﴿He shows you the lightning﴾ [al-Ra'd: 12], and what occurs in the atmosphere is, for the most part, fire and wind. So He mentioned the winds here as a reminder and confirmation of the proofs. And since the wind has a benefit other than rain, while lightning has no benefit if there is no rain, He mentioned it there as a source of fear and hope, that is, it may occur or may not occur. And He mentioned here ﴿bearers of good news﴾, because the moderating of the air or its purification by the wind is a necessary matter, and His judgment concerning it is a firm judgment.

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We certainly sent messengers before you to their peoples, and they brought them clear proofs. Then We took retribution against those who committed crime, and it was incumbent upon Us to help the believers.﴾

When He had explained the two foundations with proofs, He mentioned the third foundation, which is prophethood, and said: ﴿And We certainly sent messengers before you﴾, meaning: their being sent is a proof of your messengership. For they had no concern other than yours, and nothing appeared upon them other than what appeared upon you. Those who lied about them were struck with ruin, and whoever believed in them had victory for themselves. There is another aspect that shows the connection of this verse to what precedes it: when Allah had explained the proofs and the disbelievers did not benefit from them, He consoled the heart of the Prophet ﷺ and said: The condition of those who came before you was like this, and they also brought clear proofs, and among their peoples there were disbelievers and believers, just as among your people. So We took retribution against the disbelievers and granted victory to the believers. Regarding His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And it was incumbent﴾ there are two aspects:

The first: ﴿So We took retribution﴾, and the retribution was incumbent (ḥaqqan), and then He resumed and said, ﴿upon Us was the help of the believers﴾. On this reading, this is good news for the believers who believed in Muhammad ﷺ, meaning: upon Us is your victory, O believers.

The second aspect: ﴿And it was incumbent upon Us﴾, meaning the help of the believers was incumbent upon Us. On the first reading there is a subtle point, and on the second there is another. As for the first, when He said "So We took retribution," He made clear that it was not oppression but was rather justice and truth. This is because retribution was only taken after their continued existence had become productive of nothing but increased sin and the begetting of a wicked, profligate disbeliever, and their non-existence was better than their corrupt existence. As for the second, it emphasizes the good news, because the word ʿalā (upon) conveys the meaning of obligation; one says "upon so-and-so is such-and-such," which indicates obligation. When He said ḥaqqan (truly), it emphasized that meaning. We have already mentioned that victory is the dominance whose outcome is not disastrous. If one of the two groups is defeated at first and then returns at the end, victory belongs only to the one who was defeated. Likewise Moses and his people, when they were defeated by Pharaoh and then drowning overtook him, their defeat was nothing but victory. So if a disbeliever defeats a Muslim at some times, that is not victory, since it has no outcome.

Then Allah, the Exalted, said:

﴿It is Allah who sends the winds, and they stir up clouds, and He spreads them in the sky however He wills, and makes them into fragments, and you see the rain coming out from within them. Then He, exalted, said: ﴿And if We sent a wind and they saw it turn yellow, they would surely continue to disbelieve after it.﴾ ﴿So indeed you cannot make the dead hear, nor can you make the deaf hear the call when they turn away, retreating.﴾ ﴿And you are not a guide for the blind away from their misguidance. The first issue: In the first verse He said ﴿He sends the winds﴾ in the form of reporting the sending, but here He said ﴿And if We send﴾, not in the form of reporting the sending. This is because the winds are from His mercy and are frequent, whereas the wind is from His punishment. And He, exalted, is Compassionate toward His servants, and He restrains it. For this reason we see the beneficial winds blowing during the nights and days, across the open deserts and the hills, whereas the simoom (scorching wind) blows only at certain times and in certain places.

The second issue: He called the beneficial ones "winds" (plural) and the harmful one "wind" (singular), for several reasons.

One: The beneficial winds are many in kind and many in instances, so He used the plural. Every day and night, breezes of beneficial winds blow, whereas the harmful wind does not blow for years; rather, harmful winds generally do not blow for ages.

Two: Beneficial winds are never a single wind, for what blows only once does not purify the air, does not produce clouds, and does not move ships. As for the harmful one, a single gust can kill, like the simoom.

This does not happen to the wind in its blowing; it happens because the air that is stagnant in a patch containing bad vegetation, or in a low-lying place, is extremely hot, or because it is formed in that same state at the start of its formation. In either case it is a single occurrence, because when that stagnant air is heated and then a wind reaches it and stirs it and drives it out of that place, it blows over places like a flame. Whatever comes out of that place afterward is neither hot nor poisoned, because long lingering is a condition for taking on a quality. Do you not see that if you put your finger into a fire and take it out quickly, it is not affected, whereas iron that remains in it melts? So when that stagnant air moves and disperses, nothing of its kind exists at that moment except it. As for what is generated in this way, it is rare, and the place of its rarity is one. As for quantity, when winds gather and become one, they become like a torrent, and the waters of springs, when gathered, become a great river that dams cannot block and boulders cannot turn back. There is no doubt that in this case it is one gathered from many. For this reason He said "a wind" for the harmful one and "winds" for the beneficial ones.

Therefore, dealing with the blind is easier than dealing with the deaf who hears nothing, because the ultimate form of conveying meaning is by speech. Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿It is Allah who created you from weakness, then made after weakness strength, then made after strength weakness and gray hair. He creates what He wills, and He is the All-Knowing, the All-Powerful.﴾

When He had repeated, among the proofs mentioned earlier, one proof from the signs of the horizons, which is His saying: ﴿It is Allah who sends the winds, so they stir up clouds﴾, and had mentioned the states of the wind from beginning to end, He repeated a proof from the signs within the souls, which is the creation of the human being, and mentioned his states. So He said: ﴿created you from weakness﴾, meaning, your foundation is upon weakness, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Man was created of haste﴾ [al-Anbiya': 37]. And "min" here is like in the saying of the speaker: "So-and-so adorned so-and-so from his poverty and made him rich", meaning, from his state of poverty. Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿then made after weakness strength﴾. So His saying ﴿from weakness﴾ points to a state in which he was a fetus, an infant, a newborn, and one weaned. These are the states of utmost weakness. His saying ﴿then made after weakness strength﴾ points to the state of his reaching maturity, his vigor, his youth, and his reaching middle age. His saying ﴿then made after strength weakness and gray hair. He creates what He wills, and He is the All-Knowing, the All-Powerful﴾

points to what comes after middle age of the appearance of decline. "Shaybah" (gray hair/old age) is the completion of weakness. Then by His saying ﴿He creates what He wills﴾ He made clear that this is not by nature, but by the will of Allah, exalted is He, as He said regarding the signs of the horizons: ﴿and spreads it in the sky however He wills﴾ ﴿And He is the All-Knowing, the All-Powerful﴾. Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 30, verse 56:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those who were given knowledge and faith will say: "You have remained, according to the Book of Allah, until the Day of Resurrection. So this is the Day of Resurrection, but you did not know."﴾

His saying: ﴿And those who were given knowledge and faith﴾ — from among the angels and others — ﴿will say: "You have remained, according to the Book of Allah, until the Day of Resurrection."﴾ We will explain what the subtle meaning is in these two verses, so we say: The one who is promised a promise, when a term is set for him, considers the term long and wishes to hasten it. The one who is threatened with a threat, when a term is set for him, considers the period short and wishes to delay it. But the criminal, when he is gathered, knows that his destination is the Fire, so he considers the duration of his stay small and chooses to delay the gathering and to remain in the grave. The believer, when he is gathered, knows that his destination is Paradise, so he considers the duration great and does not wish for delay. Thus the two groups differ. One of them says: "The duration of our stay is short," and to this refers His saying: ﴿The criminals will swear that they had not stayed but an hour﴾. The other says: "We stayed a long time," and to this refers His exalted saying: ﴿And those who were given knowledge and faith will say: "You have remained, according to the Book of Allah, until the Day of Resurrection."﴾ That is, the term set in the Book of Allah was until the Day of Resurrection, and we have waited until the Day of Resurrection. ﴿So this is the Day of Resurrection, but you did not know.﴾ That is, your seeking of delay: you did not know the Resurrection and did not acknowledge it, so your destination became the Fire, and therefore you seek delay.

Then He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿So on that Day, those who did wrong will not benefit from their excuse, nor will they be asked to make amends.﴾ That is, they will not be asked for i'tab, which is the removal of blame, meaning: the repentance that removes the traces of the wrongdoing will not be sought from them, because it will not be accepted from them.

Indeed, it is not permissible for the one presenting an argument, after having stated a good, sound, clear proof that has no flaw, and his opponent has been obstinate, to begin another proof. This is because he either acknowledges that the opponent's objection to it is valid or he does not acknowledge it. If he acknowledges it, that is a cutting off (inqita') and it discredits either the proof or the one presenting it, either by showing that the proof is invalid or that the one presenting it is ignorant of the manner of indication and inference; and neither of these may be acknowledged by a scholar, so how much less by a Prophet, peace be upon him. And if he does not acknowledge it, then beginning another proof gives the impression that the opponent is not obstinate, so his boldness in obstinacy becomes greater in the second case, because he says: "Obstinacy has benefited me in the first case, since he committed himself to mentioning another proof." If it is said: The Prophets, peace be upon them, mentioned various kinds of proofs; we say, they recited them in a sequence, then established them one by one, like one who says: "The proof for this is from several aspects: the first is such-and-such, the second is such-and-such, the third is such-and-such." In such a case, it is obligatory not to pay attention to the obstinacy of the obstinate, because he increases in his obstinacy until time is wasted, so the one presenting the proof cannot complete all the proofs he promised, and his standing is lowered. Therefore, for every situation there is a suitable statement. We say: The meaning is that whoever does not know now, God has already sealed his heart beforehand.
